atom 25 · sequential traversal

SEQUENTIAL TRAVERSAL — THE CANONICAL FOR LOOP

unit3_atom_025.c
#define  N 6
int data[N] = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42};

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    printf("Element %d = %d\n", i, data[i]);
}
CANONICAL TRAVERSAL
The standard for loop visits every element in sequence from index 0 up to index N-1.
COMPLEXITY O(N)
Linear time: Visiting every element in an array of size N requires exactly N iterations.
atom 26 · array input loop

READING INTO ARRAYS — SCANF & ADDRESS PASSING

unit3_atom_026.c
#define  N 5
int numbers[N];

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    printf("Enter element %d: ", i);
    scanf("%d", &numbers[i]); /* Must pass address &numbers[i]! */
}
THE & OPERATOR MANDATORY
`scanf` requires a pointer. We pass `&numbers[i]`, the memory address of the specific cell being populated.
EQUIVALENCE
`&numbers[i]` is identical to writing `(numbers + i)`. Both pass the exact memory address to scanf.
atom 27 · formatted display

DISPLAYING ARRAYS — FORMATTED PRINTING

unit3_atom_027.c
void print_array(const int arr[], int size) {
    printf("[ ");
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d%s", arr[i], (i == size - 1) ? "" : ", ");
    }
    printf(" ]\n");
}
ELEGANT COMMA HANDLING
The ternary operator `(i == size - 1) ? "" : ", "` prints clean commas between numbers without a trailing comma at the end.
OUTPUT: [ 10, 20, 30 ]
Standard bracketed representation used across modern debugging utilities.
atom 28 · array sum

ARRAY ACCUMULATOR — COMPUTING TOTAL SUM

unit3_atom_028.c
int sum_array(const int arr[], int size) {
    int sum = 0; /* CRITICAL: Initialize accumulator to zero! */
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        sum += arr[i];
    }
    return sum;
}
ACCUMULATOR PATTERN
A running total variable initialized to 0. Each iteration adds one element to the accumulator.
ZERO INITIALIZATION
Failing to initialize `sum = 0` produces undefined garbage because local stack variables start with random memory bits.
atom 29 · array average

ARRAY AVERAGE — PREVENTING INTEGER TRUNCATION

unit3_atom_029.c
double average_array(const int arr[], int size) {
    if (size == 0) return 0.0; /* Guard against divide by zero */
    
    int sum = sum_array(arr, size);
    /* MUST CAST to double before division! */
    return (double)sum / size;
}
INTEGER DIVISION TRAP
`sum / size` performs integer division, discarding all decimal fractions! Write `(double)sum / size`.
ZERO SIZE GUARD
A defensive guard prevents a fatal hardware division-by-zero exception if an empty array is passed.
atom 30 · finding maximum

FINDING EXTREMA — THE MAXIMUM ELEMENT

unit3_atom_030.c
int find_max(const int arr[], int size) {
    int max_val = arr[0]; /* Initialize to FIRST element! */
    int max_idx = 0;
    
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) { // Start at index 1
        if (arr[i] > max_val) {
            max_val = arr[i];
            max_idx = i;
        }
    }
    return max_val;
}
INITIALIZE TO ARR[0]
Never initialize `max_val = 0`! If the array contains negative numbers `{-10, -5, -20}`, 0 would be incorrectly reported as max!
SKIP FIRST ITERATION
Since `max_val` holds `arr[0]`, the for-loop begins comparison at index `1`, saving one useless comparison.
atom 31 · finding minimum

FINDING EXTREMA — THE MINIMUM ELEMENT

unit3_atom_031.c
int find_min_index(const int arr[], int size) {
    int min_idx = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] < arr[min_idx]) {
            min_idx = i;
        }
    }
    return min_idx; /* Returns position of minimum */
}
INDEX TRACKING
Tracking the index `min_idx` gives you BOTH the position AND the value (`arr[min_idx]`) simultaneously.
TIE-BREAKING
Using `<` keeps the FIRST occurrence of the minimum value. Using `<=` would update to the LAST occurrence.
atom 32 · in place reversal

IN-PLACE REVERSAL — TWO-POINTER SWAP

unit3_atom_032.c
void reverse_array(int arr[], int size) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    
    while (left < right) {
        int temp = arr[left];
        arr[left] = arr[right];
        arr[right] = temp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}
TWO-POINTER ALGORITHM
Left pointer advances forward, right pointer moves backward. Elements swap until pointers meet in the center.
O(N/2) SWAPS, O(1) SPACE
Reverses the array directly in-place without allocating a second scratch buffer. Optimal memory efficiency.
atom 33 · frequency counting

FREQUENCY COUNTING — TARGET OCCURRENCES

unit3_atom_033.c
int count_occurrences(const int arr[], int size, int target) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) count++;
    }
    return count;
}
SELECTIVE ACCUMULATOR
The counter increments only when the current element satisfies the equivalence filter `arr[i] == target`.
LINEAR SCAN
Scans the full length O(N) to ensure all matching duplicates are counted.
atom 34 · insertion at index

ARRAY INSERTION — THE RIGHT-SHIFT ALGORITHM

unit3_atom_034.c
int insert_at(int arr[], int *size, int capacity, int idx, int val) {
    if (*size >= capacity || idx < 0 || idx > *size) return 0; // Fail
    
    /* Shift elements RIGHT starting from the back */
    for (int i = *size; i > idx; i--) {
        arr[i] = arr[i - 1];
    }
    arr[idx] = val;
    (*size)++;
    return 1; // Success
}
SHIFT FROM THE BACK
Crucial algorithmic detail: To insert at index `k`, shift elements backward from `size` down to `k`. Shifting forward would overwrite data!
CAPACITY CHECK
Fixed arrays cannot grow past allocated capacity. Verify `*size < capacity` before attempting insert.
atom 35 · deletion from index

ARRAY DELETION — THE LEFT-SHIFT ALGORITHM

unit3_atom_035.c
int delete_at(int arr[], int *size, int idx) {
    if (idx < 0 || idx >= *size) return 0; // Fail
    
    /* Shift elements LEFT over the deleted spot */
    for (int i = idx; i < *size - 1; i++) {
        arr[i] = arr[i + 1];
    }
    (*size)--;
    return 1; // Success
}
SHIFT FORWARD TO COMPACT
To delete index `k`, copy each element from `k+1` forward into `k`. Overwrites the target without leaving a gap.
DECREMENT SIZE
Decrement `*size` to mark the array as one element shorter. The old last element becomes dead scratch.
atom 36 · array rotation

ARRAY ROTATION — CYCLIC SHIFT

unit3_atom_036.c
/* Rotate array left by 1 position */
void rotate_left_one(int arr[], int size) {
    if (size <= 1) return;
    int first = arr[0];
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        arr[i] = arr[i + 1];
    }
    arr[size - 1] = first; // Wrap around
}
WRAP-AROUND LOGIC
Preserves the head element, shifts all remaining elements left by 1, and restores the head to the tail.
ROTATING BY K
Rotating by `K` positions can be achieved by repeating this `K` times or using the 3-reversal algorithm in O(N) time.
atom 37 · prefix sums

PREFIX SUMS — CUMULATIVE RANGE QUERIES

unit3_atom_037.c
/* Build Prefix Sum Array */
void build_prefix(const int arr[], int pref[], int size) {
    pref[0] = arr[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        pref[i] = pref[i - 1] + arr[i];
    }
}
// Range sum [L, R] = pref[R] - pref[L - 1] in O(1) time!
O(1) RANGE SUMS
Precomputing cumulative sums allows querying the sum of any subarray between indices L and R in a single subtraction!
ALGORITHMIC ACCELERATION
Widely used in graphics, image processing (integral images), and competitive programming.

By treating data values as indices into a tally array, we count all frequencies in a single O(N) pass.
ZERO SEARCH OVERHEAD
No nested loops needed. Updating counts is a direct O(1) memory increment.

atom 41 · element as argument

PASSING ELEMENTS — SCALAR VALUE PASSING

unit3_atom_041.c
void inspect_value(int val) {
    printf("Processing: %d\n", val);
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[5] = {88, 92, 79, 95, 84};
    inspect_value(scores[2]); // Passes scalar value 79 by copy!
    return 0;
}
SCALAR COPY MECHANISM
Passing `scores[i]` passes a single isolated primitive value. Follows standard Call-by-Value rules.
CALLEE CANNOT MUTATE
Modifying `val` inside `inspect_value()` has zero effect on `scores[2]` in main.
atom 42 · element address as argument

PASSING ELEMENT ADDRESS — MUTATING SPECIFIC CELLS

unit3_atom_042.c
void double_val(int *p) {
    *p *= 2;
}

int main(void) {
    int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};
    double_val(&a[1]); // Pass address of element at index 1
    printf("a[1] is now: %d\n", a[1]); // 40!
    return 0;
}
TARGETED MUTATION
By passing `&a[i]`, we give the function pointer access to modify that specific slot in the array.
POINTER EQUIVALENCE
`&a[1]` is identical to `(a + 1)`. Both produce a pointer to the second array cell.
atom 43 · whole array arguments

PASSING WHOLE ARRAYS — POINTER DECAY MECHANISM

unit3_atom_043.c
/* In C, an array argument DECAYS into a pointer! */
void print_all(int arr[], int size) {
    // Under the hood, 'int arr[]' IS ACTUALLY 'int *arr'!
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
}
ARRAY-TO-POINTER DECAY
In C, an array name passed as a function argument instantly decays into a pointer to its first element (`&arr[0]`).
NO COPY OVERHEAD
C NEVER copies entire arrays onto stack frames! Passing a million-element array takes 8 bytes of address overhead.
atom 44 · sizeof decay trap

THE SIZEOF DECAY TRAP — POINTER SIZE vs ARRAY SIZE

unit3_atom_044.c
void bad_size_calc(int arr[]) {
    /* FATAL BUG: sizeof(arr) returns POINTER SIZE (8 bytes)! */
    size_t count = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]); // 8 / 4 = 2!
    printf("Count reported: %zu\n", count); // Always 2 on 64-bit!
}
DECAYED SIZEOF
Inside a function parameter list, `sizeof(arr)` evaluates to `sizeof(int*)`, which is 8 bytes regardless of original array capacity!
MANDATORY SIZE ARGUMENT
Because arrays do not carry their own length metadata, you MUST ALWAYS pass the array size as a separate parameter!

}

// Caller: process_data(my_arr, 100);

Virtually every C array function requires two parameters: (1) The pointer/array `arr[]`, and (2) The integer `size`.

atom 46 · mutating array elements

MUTATING ARRAY ELEMENTS — AUTOMATIC BY-REFERENCE EFFECT

unit3_atom_046.c
void zero_out(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        arr[i] = 0; /* DIRECTLY MODIFIES CALLER'S MEMORY! */
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[3] = {1, 2, 3};
    zero_out(data, 3); // data is now {0, 0, 0} in main!
}
AUTOMATIC BY-REFERENCE
Because `arr` is a pointer to the caller's original buffer, assigning `arr[i] = 0` directly mutates the caller's memory!
NO & NEEDED AT CALL SITE
Notice caller writes `zero_out(data, 3)`. The array name `data` already evaluates to its own base address.

CONST ARRAY PARAMETERS — READ-ONLY PROTECTION

/* Promise the caller: This function will NOT mutate your data */
int find_sum(const int arr[], int size) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        sum += arr[i];
        // arr[i] = 0; // COMPILE ERROR! Read-only location!
    }
    return sum;
}
THE CONST CONTRACT
Prefixing `const int arr[]` informs both the compiler and code reviewers that this function strictly reads data.
ACCIDENTAL MUTATION GUARD
If you accidentally write `if (arr[i] = 0)` instead of `==`, the compiler flags it immediately as an illegal assignment.

atom 53 · searching overview

SEARCHING AN ARRAY — THE SEARCH PROBLEM

unit3_atom_053.c
/* Given array A of size N and target value X: */
// Return index i where A[i] == X, or -1 if not found.

// Two Fundamental Approaches:
// 1. Linear Search: Works on ANY array (Unsorted or Sorted)
// 2. Binary Search: Requires array to be PRE-SORTED!
THE CORE OPERATION
Searching is the most frequent computational operation in software engineering (database lookups, symbol tables, UI filtering).
PRECONDITION MATTERS
You cannot use binary search on arbitrary random data. It strictly requires sorted ordering.
atom 54 · linear search algorithm

LINEAR SEARCH — SEQUENTIAL SCANNING

unit3_atom_054.c
int linear_search(const int arr[], int size, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) {
            return i; /* Match found: Return index immediately */
        }
    }
    return -1; /* Match not found after full scan */
}
EARLY EXIT ON MATCH
If the target is at index 0, the function exits in O(1) time. If absent, it checks all N elements before returning -1.
COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS
Best case: O(1). Worst case: O(N). Average case: O(N/2) comparisons. Simple, universal, zero memory overhead.
atom 55 · sentinel search

SENTINEL LINEAR SEARCH — OPTIMIZING LOOP BOUNDS

unit3_atom_055.c
int sentinel_search(int arr[], int size, int target) {
    int last = arr[size - 1];
    arr[size - 1] = target; /* Place target as sentinel at end */
    
    int i = 0;
    while (arr[i] != target) i++; /* NO 'i < size' BOUNDS CHECK! */
    
    arr[size - 1] = last; /* Restore original value */
    if (i < size - 1 || last == target) return i;
    return -1;
}
ELIMINATES BOUNDS CHECK
By guaranteeing the target exists at the end, the inner while loop only tests `arr[i] != target`, cutting loop branch tests in half!
CLASSIC C OPTIMIZATION
Pioneered by Donald Knuth. Saves millions of CPU instructions on large array scans.
atom 56 · binary search concept

BINARY SEARCH (FIRST LOOK) — DIVIDE AND CONQUER

unit3_atom_056.c
/* PRECONDITION: Array must be SORTED! */
// Target: 42 in {10, 20, 30, 42, 50, 60, 70, 80}
// Step 1: Check middle (42 vs 42) -> Found in 1 comparison!

// Halves the search space every single iteration: N -> N/2 -> N/4 -> 1
LOGARITHMIC POWER
Searching 1,000,000 elements with Linear Search takes up to 1,000,000 steps. Binary Search takes at most 20 steps!
O(log N) EFFICIENCY
log2(1,000,000) ≈ 20. log2(4,000,000,000) ≈ 32. Scales effortlessly to massive datasets.
atom 57 · binary search implementation

BINARY SEARCH CODE (FIRST LOOK) — MIDPOINT CALCULATION

unit3_atom_057.c
int binary_search(const int arr[], int size, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = size - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; /* Safe midpoint */
        if (arr[mid] == target)      return mid; // Match!
        else if (arr[mid] < target)  low = mid + 1;  // Search right half
        else                         high = mid - 1; // Search left half
    }
    return -1; // Not found
}
OVERFLOW-SAFE MIDPOINT
Never write `(low + high) / 2`! If low and high are large, their sum overflows integer bounds. Write `low + (high - low) / 2`.
BOUNDS UPDATES
Notice `low = mid + 1` and `high = mid - 1`. The midpoint has already been verified, so it must be excluded from subsequent windows.
atom 58 · binary search trace

BINARY SEARCH TRACE (FIRST LOOK) — STEP-BY-STEP TRACE

unit3_atom_058.c
/* Searching for 70 in: {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90} (size 9) */
// Iter 1: low=0, high=8, mid=4 (val=50). 70 > 50 -> low = 5
// Iter 2: low=5, high=8, mid=6 (val=70). 70 == 70 -> MATCH at index 6!
// Completed in exactly 2 comparisons!
WINDOW HALVING
In iteration 1, half the entire array ({10, 20, 30, 40, 50}) is discarded permanently.
TERMINATION CONDITION
If the target is absent, `low` eventually surpasses `high` (`low > high`), gracefully exiting the while loop.

ORDER CREATES SPEED
Sorted arrays enable O(log N) binary search and high-speed data compression and deduplication.
ELEMENTARY SORTS
Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, and Insertion Sort: Simple, in-place O(N^2) algorithms foundational to computer science.
atom 60 · bubble sort algorithm

BUBBLE SORT — ADJACENT PAIR COMPARISONS

unit3_atom_060.c
void bubble_sort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                /* Swap adjacent out-of-order elements */
                int temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }
}
BUBBLING MECHANISM
In each outer pass `i`, the largest remaining unsorted element bubbles up to its permanent home at the end of the array.
INNER LIMIT: size - 1 - i
Notice the inner loop stops at `size - 1 - i` because the last `i` elements are already guaranteed to be in final sorted order!
atom 61 · bubble sort trace

BUBBLE SORT TRACE — PASS-BY-PASS STATE

unit3_atom_061.c
/* Initial: { 5, 1, 4, 2, 8 } */
// Pass 1: (5,1)->{1,5,4,2,8} -> (5,4)->{1,4,5,2,8} -> (5,2)->{1,4,2,5,8}
//         (5,8)->{1,4,2,5,8} [8 is now locked at the end!]
// Pass 2: { 1, 2, 4, 5, 8 }   [5 is locked]
// Pass 3: Array is sorted!
N-1 TOTAL PASSES
An array of size N requires at most N - 1 outer passes to guarantee 100% sorted ordering.
STABILITY GUARANTEED
Because it only swaps strictly greater elements `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, duplicates preserve their original relative order.
atom 62 · optimized bubble sort

OPTIMIZED BUBBLE SORT — EARLY TERMINATION FLAG

unit3_atom_062.c
void bubble_sort_opt(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int swapped = 0; /* Flag tracking swaps */
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                int t = arr[j]; arr[j] = arr[j+1]; arr[j+1] = t;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }
        if (swapped == 0) break; /* Already sorted! Exit early! */
    }
}
O(N) BEST CASE
If the input array is already sorted, the inner loop completes with 0 swaps. The flag triggers an immediate early exit!
ADAPTIVE SPEED
Cuts execution time dramatically on nearly-sorted data.
atom 63 · selection sort first look

SELECTION SORT — MINIMUM EXTRACTION

unit3_atom_063.c
void selection_sort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int min_idx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (arr[j] < arr[min_idx]) min_idx = j;
        }
        /* Exactly ONE swap per outer pass! */
        int temp = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[min_idx]; arr[min_idx] = temp;
    }
}
MINIMUM DATA MOVEMENT
Finds the smallest item in the unsorted suffix and swaps it directly into index `i`. Executes at most N - 1 swaps total!
EXCELLENT FOR FLASH MEMORY
Ideal for systems where writing to memory is expensive or degrades hardware life.
atom 64 · insertion sort first look

INSERTION SORT — PLAYING CARD ANALOGY

unit3_atom_064.c
void insertion_sort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        int key = arr[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) {
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]; // Shift right
            j--;
        }
        arr[j + 1] = key;
    }
}
CARD PLAYER'S METHOD
Picks up element `key` and shifts larger elements to the right to insert the key into its correct sorted prefix position.
SUPERIOR FOR SMALL DATA
Outperforms QuickSort and MergeSort on small arrays (N < 20). Standard hybrid sort leaf component.

atom 77 · row major layout

ROW-MAJOR ORDER — FLAT RAM LAYOUT

unit3_atom_077.c
/* C stores 2D arrays in ROW-MAJOR order! */
// matrix[2][3] memory sequence:
// [ Row 0, Col 0 ] -> address 0x100
// [ Row 0, Col 1 ] -> address 0x104
// [ Row 0, Col 2 ] -> address 0x108
// [ Row 1, Col 0 ] -> address 0x10C (Adjacent in RAM!)
// [ Row 1, Col 1 ] -> address 0x110
// [ Row 1, Col 2 ] -> address 0x114
ROW-MAJOR RULE
Row 0 is laid out in physical RAM first, followed immediately by Row 1, Row 2, etc.
FORTRAN vs C
C is Row-Major; Fortran and MATLAB are Column-Major. Critical for scientific programming interop.
atom 78 · address calculation formula

ADDRESS CALCULATION — O(1) 2D MAPPING

unit3_atom_078.c
/* Address formula for matrix[R][C] at position [i][j]: */
// Address = Base + (i * C + j) * sizeof(type)

// Notice 'C' (Number of Columns) is strictly required to skip rows!
// 'R' (Number of Rows) is NOT needed for the offset calculation!
THE i * C + j FORMULA
To skip `i` rows, the hardware jumps `i * C` elements ahead, then adds `j` column steps.
WHY COLUMNS MATTER
This explains why function prototypes require the column dimension: `func(int m[][COLS])`.

atom 80 · cache locality traversal

CACHE LOCALITY — ROW vs COLUMN MAJOR SWEEP

unit3_atom_080.c
/* FAST: Row-by-Row (Traverses consecutive memory cells) */
for (int r = 0; r < R; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) sum += m[r][c];

/* SLOW: Column-by-Column (Strides across RAM, cache misses!) */
for (int c = 0; c < C; c++)
    for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) sum += m[r][c];
CPU CACHE LINES
Hardware caches load 64-byte blocks of adjacent RAM. Sweeping row-major hits cache on every step (10x faster!).
STRIDED PENALTY
Sweeping column-major skips `C` integers on each step, causing constant cache thrashing and memory bus delays.
atom 81 · matrix addition

MATRIX ADDITION — ELEMENT-WISE SUM

unit3_atom_081.c
void add_matrices(int R, int C, const int A[R][C], 
                  const int B[R][C], int Out[R][C]) {
    for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) {
            Out[r][c] = A[r][c] + B[r][c];
        }
    }
}
DIMENSION EQUALITY
Matrix addition requires matrices A and B to share the identical row and column dimensions.
O(R * C) COMPLEXITY
Direct linear traversal over all R*C cells. Simple, clean, parallelizable.
atom 82 · matrix transpose

MATRIX TRANSPOSE — SWAPPING ROWS & COLS

unit3_atom_082.c
/* Transpose square matrix in-place */
void transpose(int N, int m[N][N]) {
    for (int r = 0; r < N; r++) {
        for (int c = r + 1; c < N; c++) { // Upper triangle only!
            int temp = m[r][c];
            m[r][c] = m[c][r];
            m[c][r] = temp;
        }
    }
}
UPPER TRIANGLE SWAP
Notice inner loop starts at `c = r + 1`. Swapping only the upper triangle reflects elements across the main diagonal.
AVOIDING DOUBLE SWAP
Running from `c = 0` would swap elements and then swap them right back to original positions!
atom 83 · matrix multiplication

MATRIX MULTIPLICATION — THE 3-LOOP ALGORITHM

unit3_atom_083.c
/* Multiply A (M x K) by B (K x N) -> Result C (M x N) */
void matrix_multiply(int M, int K, int N, 
                     const int A[M][K], const int B[K][N], int C_out[M][N]) {
    for (int i = 0; i < M; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            C_out[i][j] = 0;
            for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {
                C_out[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]; // Dot product!
            }
        }
    }
}
THE 3 NESTED LOOPS
Loops `i` and `j` select the output cell. Innermost loop `k` computes the vector dot product of row `i` and column `j`.
O(M * K * N) COMPLEXITY
Cubic complexity: Multiplying two 1000x1000 matrices requires 1,000,000,000 multiplications! Foundation of graphics and AI.
atom 84 · identity matrix

IDENTITY MATRIX — KRONECKER DELTA

unit3_atom_084.c
void make_identity(int N, int m[N][N]) {
    for (int r = 0; r < N; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < N; c++) {
            m[r][c] = (r == c) ? 1 : 0; // 1 on main diagonal, 0 elsewhere
        }
    }
}
MAIN DIAGONAL
Elements where row index equals column index (`r == c`) form the main diagonal.
MULTIPLICATIVE NEUTRAL
Multiplying any matrix by the Identity matrix `I` yields the original matrix unchanged (`A * I = A`).
atom 85 · row & col sums

ROW & COLUMN SUMS — MARGINAL ACCUMULATION

unit3_atom_085.c
void compute_marginal_sums(int R, int C, const int m[R][C]) {
    for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) {
        int r_sum = 0;
        for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) r_sum += m[r][c];
        printf("Row %d sum = %d\n", r, r_sum);
    }
}
RESET ACCUMULATOR
Notice `r_sum = 0` is placed INSIDE the outer loop to reset the total for each new row.
CROSS-SECTION ANALYSIS
Allows computing subtotals across spreadsheet rows or accounting ledger columns.

2D ARRAY PITFALLS — INVERTED INDICES

THE R vs C TRAP
Always verify: `for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++)` and `for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++)`.
BRACKET SYNTAX
Never write `table[r, c]`. C requires separate brackets: `table[r][c]`.

atom 89 · string definition

STRING BASICS — NULL-TERMINATED CHAR ARRAYS

unit3_atom_089.c
/* A string in C is a char array terminated by '\0' */
char greeting[6] = {'H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o', '\0'};

/* Equivalent string literal shortcut: */
char greeting_lit[] = "Hello"; // Compiler automatically appends '\0'!
THE NULL TERMINATOR (\0)
ASCII code 0 (`0x00`). Signals the exact end of a string in memory without needing a separate length variable.
THE +1 BYTE RULE
A word with 5 letters ("Hello") requires AT LEAST 6 bytes of storage in RAM to accommodate the null terminator!
atom 90 · string declarations

STRING DECLARATIONS — ARRAY vs POINTER

unit3_atom_090.c
/* Style 1: Mutable Character Array (Stack allocated) */
char s1[] = "Hello";
s1[0] = 'h'; // Legal! Modifies stack copy to "hello"

/* Style 2: Pointer to String Literal (Rodata read-only) */
char *s2 = "Hello";
// s2[0] = 'h'; // CRASH! Segmentation Fault (Bus Error)!
MUTABLE STACK ARRAY
`char s[] = "text";` copies characters onto the local stack frame where they can be freely modified.
READ-ONLY LITERAL
`char *s = "text";` points directly to the read-only data segment (`.rodata`). Writing to it triggers an OS memory protection crash!
atom 91 · memory layout of strings

STRING MEMORY MAP — BYTE VISUALIZATION

unit3_atom_091.c
/* Memory map of char str[8] = "C-DEV"; */
// Index:    [0]  [1]  [2]  [3]  [4]  [5]  [6]  [7]
// Char:     'C'  '-'  'D'  'E'  'V' '\0'  ?    ?
// ASCII:     67   45   68   69   86    0   --   --
// strlen(str) = 5 (characters before '\0')
// sizeof(str) = 8 (total allocated bytes in RAM)
STRLEN vs SIZEOF
`strlen()` counts characters up to (excluding) `\0`. `sizeof()` returns the full capacity of the allocated array.
SENTINEL BARRIER
Standard string functions read sequentially until hitting `\0` and stop immediately, ignoring any remaining garbage cells.
atom 92 · printing strings

PRINTING STRINGS — THE %s SPECIFIER

unit3_atom_092.c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    char msg[] = "Antigravity Terminal";
    printf("%s\n", msg);     // Prints until '\0'
    puts(msg);               // Automatically appends newline
    return 0;
}
%s PRINTF MECHANICS
`printf("%s", ptr)` dereferences bytes one-by-one and prints them to console until encountering byte 0 (`\0`).
MISSING NULL CATASTROPHE
If a char array lacks `\0`, `%s` continues reading past the array into random RAM, printing gibberish until hitting a random 0 or crashing!
atom 93 · reading strings scanf

READING STRINGS — SCANF & SPACE TRUNCATION

unit3_atom_093.c
char name[20];
printf("Enter name: ");
scanf("%s", name); /* NOTE: NO & here! 'name' IS an address! */

// User types: "Dennis Ritchie"
// name stores: "Dennis" (Truncates at first whitespace!)
NO & NEEDED
Because array names decay to addresses, writing `&name` in scanf is redundant. Simply write `name`.
WHITESPACE DELIMITER
`%s` in scanf stops reading at the first space, tab, or newline! Cannot read full names or sentences.
atom 94 · safe input fgets

SAFE INPUT: FGETS — PREVENTING BUFFER OVERFLOW

unit3_atom_094.c
#include <stdio.h>
#define  MAX 64

int main(void) {
    char buffer[MAX];
    printf("Enter full text: ");
    
    /* Safe: Reads up to MAX-1 chars, preserves spaces! */
    if (fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin) != NULL) {
        printf("Received: %s", buffer);
    }
    return 0;
}
THE GOLD STANDARD
`fgets(buf, size, stdin)` is the only safe way to read strings in C. It guarantees never reading more than `size - 1` bytes.
NEVER USE GETS()
The ancient `gets()` function has no size parameter and caused billions of dollars in hacker exploits. Removed from standard C!
atom 95 · stripping newline

NEWLINE STRIPPING — THE FGETS CLEANUP IDIOM

unit3_atom_095.c
#include <string.h>

/* fgets stores the trailing '\n' when user hits Enter! */
// Canonical Idiom to strip trailing newline:
buffer[strcspn(buffer, "\r\n")] = '\0';

// Overwrites the '\n' with '\0', yielding a clean string!
FGETS NEWLINE QUIRK
When the user presses Enter, `fgets` stores the `\n` right before `\0`, causing unwanted extra linebreaks in output.
STRCSPN CLEANUP
`strcspn(buf, "\r\n")` finds the index of the newline and replaces it with `\0` in a single robust line of code.

C has no native string primitive type; strings are simply arrays of bytes with a zero terminator convention.

THE STRING ENGINE
`` provides optimized assembly implementations of standard string algorithms.

Compilers use vector SIMD instructions (AVX/SSE) inside standard library string routines for maximum throughput.
atom 98 · strlen mechanics

STRING LENGTH — STRLEN IMPLEMENTATION

unit3_atom_098.c
/* Re-implementing strlen() */
size_t my_strlen(const char *s) {
    const char *p = s;
    while (*p != '\0') {
        p++; /* Advance pointer until null terminator */
    }
    return p - s; /* Pointer difference = element count */
}
POINTER ARITHMETIC
Subtracting the starting pointer from the end pointer `p - s` computes the exact character count in O(N) time.
EXCLUDES NULL TERMINATOR
`strlen("ABC")` returns 3, even though 4 bytes are consumed in RAM.
atom 99 · string copy

STRING ASSIGNMENT — STRCPY vs ASSIGNMENT

unit3_atom_099.c
char src[] = "Data";
char dest[10];

// dest = src; // COMPILE ERROR! Cannot assign to array name!

strcpy(dest, src); /* Correct: copies bytes from src to dest */
printf("dest = %s\n", dest); // "Data"
WHY ASSIGNMENT FAILS
Array names in C are not modifiable lvalues. You cannot assign one array directly into another with `=`. You must copy bytes!
BUFFER OVERFLOW HAZARD
`strcpy(dest, src)` does not check bounds! If `src` has 50 chars and `dest` has 10, it overflows memory and crashes!
atom 100 · safe strncpy

SAFE BOUNDED COPY — STRNCPY & NULL TRAP

unit3_atom_100.c
char src[] = "Supercalifragilistic";
char dest[10];

strncpy(dest, src, sizeof(dest) - 1);
dest[sizeof(dest) - 1] = '\0'; /* CRITICAL: Force null termination! */

printf("Safe truncation: %s\n", dest); // "Supercali"
THE STRNCPY TRAP
If `src` is longer than `n`, `strncpy` DOES NOT append a `\0`! You must explicitly set `dest[size-1] = '\0';`!
DEFENSIVE SAFEGUARD
Always null-terminate explicitly to guarantee string safety after `strncpy`.

CHARACTER SEARCH — STRCHR & STRRCHR

const char *path = "/home/user/docs/report.pdf";

/* strchr: Finds FIRST occurrence */

/* strrchr: Finds LAST occurrence */
char *filename = strrchr(path, '/');    // Points to "/report.pdf"
if (filename) printf("File: %s\n", filename + 1); // "report.pdf"
POINTER RETURN
Returns a pointer directly into the original string where the character was found, or `NULL` if not found.
FILE EXTENSION EXTRACTION
`strrchr(filename, '.')` extracts file extensions (`.pdf`, `.c`) in a single line.
atom 102 · substring search

SUBSTRING SEARCH — STRSTR ALGORITHM

unit3_atom_102.c
const char *haystack = "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html";
const char *needle = "200 OK";

char *match = strstr(haystack, needle);
if (match != NULL) {
    printf("Success code found at offset: %ld\n", match - haystack);
}
SUBSTRING MATCHING
Scans `haystack` for the first occurrence of `needle`. Returns pointer to start of match, or NULL.
PARSING PROTOCOLS
Essential for parsing HTTP response headers, URLs, and incoming network packets.
atom 103 · string tokenization

STRING TOKENIZATION — STRTOK DELIMITERS

unit3_atom_103.c
char csv_line[] = "Apple,Banana,Cherry,Dates";
char *token = strtok(csv_line, ",");

while (token != NULL) {
    printf("Fruit: %s\n", token);
    token = strtok(NULL, ","); /* Pass NULL to continue parsing! */
}
MUTATES ORIGINAL STRING
`strtok` replaces delimiter commas with `\0` in-place! Never pass a string literal to strtok.
STATIC INTERNAL STATE
Passing `NULL` tells strtok to resume where it left off using an internal static pointer. Not thread-safe! Use `strtok_r` in POSIX.
atom 104 · string concatenation

STRING CONCATENATION — STRCAT & STRNCAT

unit3_atom_104.c
char greeting[30] = "Hello, ";
char name[] = "World!";

/* Appends name to end of greeting */
strcat(greeting, name); // greeting becomes "Hello, World!"

/* Safe bounded concatenation: */
strncat(greeting, " - Ready", sizeof(greeting) - strlen(greeting) - 1);
APPENDING TEXT
`strcat` finds the `\0` in destination, overwrites it with the source string, and appends a new `\0` at the end.
CAPACITY CHECK
Destination buffer must have enough allocated space for both strings plus the null terminator.

SPRINTF & SNPRINTF — BUFFER FORMATTING

`snprintf()` guarantees never writing past `sizeof(query)`. Returns the number of characters that would have been written.
POWERFUL COMPOSITION
Combines integers, floats, and strings into formatted text buffers for networking, logging, and SQL generation.

SSCANF PARSING — EXTRACTING FROM BUFFERS

`sscanf` parses data from an existing string in RAM instead of keyboard `stdin`.

atom 107 · palindrome checker

CASE STUDY: PALINDROME — TWO-POINTER STRING MATCH

unit3_atom_107.c
int is_palindrome(const char *s) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = strlen(s) - 1;
    
    while (left < right) {
        if (s[left] != s[right]) return 0; /* Mismatch! */
        left++;
        right--;
    }
    return 1; /* Palindrome confirmed! */
}
O(N/2) EFFICIENCY
Inward two-pointer traversal tests matching mirrored characters ("radar", "level").
IN-PLACE INSPECTION
Operates directly on the string without copying or reversing memory.
atom 108 · string comparison

STRING COMPARISON — STRCMP & ASCII DIFFERENCE

unit3_atom_108.c
char s1[] = "Apple";
char s2[] = "Banana";

// if (s1 == s2) // BUG: Compares memory addresses, NOT characters!

int res = strcmp(s1, s2);
if (res < 0)  printf("%s comes BEFORE %s\n", s1, s2); // "Apple" < "Banana"
if (res == 0) printf("Strings are identical\n");
if (res > 0)  printf("%s comes AFTER %s\n", s1, s2);
POINTER EQUALITY TRAP
`s1 == s2` tests if both arrays share the identical memory address! Always use `strcmp()` to compare text content.
ASCII DIFFERENCE
`strcmp` subtracts character ASCII codes: 'A' (65) - 'B' (66) = -1. Returns negative if s1 < s2.
atom 109 · lexicographical ordering

LEXICOGRAPHICAL ORDER — DICTIONARY SORTING

unit3_atom_109.c
/* Bounded Comparison with strncmp */
if (strncmp("apple_pie", "apple_cider", 5) == 0) {
    printf("Both strings share the 'apple' prefix!\n");
}

/* Sorting Strings alphabetically using strcmp in Bubble Sort: */
// if (strcmp(names[j], names[j+1]) > 0) swap_pointers();
CASE-SENSITIVITY
In standard ASCII, uppercase letters precede lowercase: "Zebra" comes BEFORE "apple"!
STRNCMP PREFIX MATCH
`strncmp(s1, s2, n)` compares only the first `n` characters. Perfect for checking command prefixes.

atom 01 · recursion definition

THE NATURE OF RECURSION — SELF-REFERENTIAL LOGIC

unit4_atom_001.c
/* A function that calls itself directly or indirectly */
void count_down(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) {             /* 1. BASE CASE (Stopping condition) */
        printf("Liftoff!\n");
        return;
    }
    printf("%d... ", n);
    count_down(n - 1);        /* 2. RECURSIVE STEP (Progresses to base) */
}
SELF-SIMILARITY
Recursion solves a complex problem by reducing it to a smaller instance of the exact same problem.
MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION
Anchored on a proven base case (P(0)), with an inductive step that transforms P(n) into P(n-1).
atom 02 · base case essential

THE BASE CASE — THE STOPPING ANCHOR

unit4_atom_002.c
/* FATAL BUG: Missing Base Case */
void infinite_recurse(int n) {
    // No 'if' check to stop!
    infinite_recurse(n - 1); // Calls forever until stack explodes!
}
// Result: SIGSEGV (Segmentation Fault: Stack Overflow)
MANDATORY ANCHOR
Every recursive function MUST possess at least one non-recursive base case that returns immediately without calling itself.
ORDER OF EXECUTION
Always place the base case check at the VERY TOP of the function body as a guard clause.
atom 03 · recursive step

THE RECURSIVE STEP — MAKING PROGRESS

unit4_atom_003.c
/* The Recursive Step MUST strictly move toward the Base Case! */
int sum_down(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return 0;       // Base case
    return n + sum_down(n - 1); // n-1 strictly moves closer to 0!
}
CONVERGENCE GUARANTEE
If the recursive argument does not make strict progress toward the base case, the function loops infinitely.
DECREASING METRIC
Every recursive step reduces a variant metric (e.g. `n`, array length, distance to target).
atom 04 · leap of faith

THE LEAP OF FAITH — THINKING RECURSIVELY

unit4_atom_004.c
/* How to write recursive code without getting dizzy: */
// 1. Assume sub_function(n - 1) WORKS CORRECTLY.
// 2. Ask: "How do I combine the solution for (n - 1) with n?"
// 3. For Factorial: n! = n * (n - 1)!
// 4. Implement exactly that relation!
DECLARATIVE CLARITY
Do not attempt to mentally trace 50 nested stack frames. Trust the inductive hypothesis that the recursive call computes the correct sub-result.
COMPOSITIONAL LOGIC
Focus purely on combining the sub-problem solution with the current element.
atom 05 · head vs tail recursion

HEAD vs TAIL RECURSION — CALL PLACEMENT

unit4_atom_005.c
/* HEAD RECURSION: Work happens on UNWINDING (after call) */
void print_ascending(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return;
    print_ascending(n - 1); /* Recursive call first */
    printf("%d ", n);        /* Work happens on way back! */
}
// print_ascending(3) prints: 1 2 3
HEAD RECURSION
The recursive call occurs before the work. Processing is deferred until the stack unwinds from the base case.
TAIL RECURSION
The recursive call is the very LAST operation in the function. Highly optimizable by compilers.
atom 06 · tail recursion concept

TAIL RECURSION — FINAL OPERATION

unit4_atom_006.c
/* TAIL RECURSION: Work happens on WINDING (before call) */
void print_descending(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return;
    printf("%d ", n);         /* Work happens BEFORE call */
    print_descending(n - 1);  /* Nothing left to do after call! */
}
// print_descending(3) prints: 3 2 1
NO POST-CALL WORK
When the recursive call returns, the caller does not perform any calculations or cleanup.
COMPILER TRANSFORMATION
Modern compilers transform tail recursion into a simple `goto` loop, eliminating stack growth completely!
atom 07 · indirect recursion

INDIRECT RECURSION — MUTUAL FUNCTION CYCLES

unit4_atom_007.c
/* Forward declarations required */
int is_even(int n);
int is_odd(int n);

int is_even(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    return is_odd(n - 1);  /* Calls is_odd */
}
int is_odd(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return is_even(n - 1); /* Calls is_even */
}
MUTUAL RECURSION
Function A calls Function B, and Function B calls Function A in a cycle until terminating at a base condition.
PARSING GRAMMARS
Widely used in recursive descent compilers (e.g. `parse_expression` calls `parse_term`, which calls `parse_expression`).
atom 08 · stack overflow anatomy

STACK OVERFLOW — EXHAUSTING THE STACK

unit4_atom_008.c
/* What causes Stack Overflow? */
// Default OS Thread Stack: 1 MB to 8 MB
// Each stack frame consumes ~32 to 64 bytes.
// Calling recurse() 200,000 times exhausts the 8 MB boundary!
// OS CPU Memory Management Unit (MMU) catches guard page fault -> CRASH!
PHYSICAL STACK LIMITS
The execution stack is fixed in size at program launch. Deep recursion rapidly exhausts available stack memory.
SIGSEGV CRASH
Unlike an infinite while-loop (which just spins CPU at 100%), runaway recursion always crashes with a segmentation fault.
atom 09 · recursion vs iteration

RECURSION vs ITERATION — THE TRADE-OFF MATRIX

unit4_atom_009.c
/* Any recursive algorithm can be converted to an iterative loop! */
// Recursion: Elegant, maps naturally to trees & divide-and-conquer.
//            Cost: Stack frame allocation, function call overhead.

// Iteration: Raw CPU speed, O(1) stack memory, no overflow risk.
//            Cost: Complex manual stack management for trees.
EXPRESSIVENESS vs SPEED
Choose recursion when problem topology is inherently recursive (trees, expressions, mazes).
CHOOSE ITERATION FOR SEQUENCES
For simple counting or linear array traversal, iterative for-loops are faster and use zero stack space.
atom 10 · nature summary

RECURSION FOUNDATION — SYNTHESIS & SUMMARY

unit4_atom_010.c
/* The 3 Golden Rules of Recursion: */
// 1. Establish clear base case(s)
// 2. Ensure recursive step strictly converges toward base
// 3. Take the leap of faith for inductive combination
// Next: Tracing the Call Stack during Execution!
ELEGANT PROBLEM SOLVING
Recursion is the hallmark of sophisticated computer science algorithms.
READY FOR TRACING
Now we examine how the hardware call stack actually behaves during execution.
atom 11 · call stack during recursion

TRACING RECURSION — THE ACTIVE FRAMES STACK

unit4_atom_011.c
int fact(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * fact(n - 1);
}
// What happens in RAM when main() calls fact(3)?
FRAME MULTIPLICATION
Each recursive call creates its own brand-new activation record with its own private copy of `n`.
COEXISTING FRAMES
When `fact(1)` is running, `fact(2)`, `fact(3)`, and `main()` are all simultaneously suspended waiting in RAM!
atom 12 · the winding phase

THE WINDING PHASE — BUILDING THE STACK

unit4_atom_012.c
/* WINDING: Pushing frames onto stack */
// Step 1: main calls fact(3)      -> Frame fact(3) pushed [n=3]
// Step 2: fact(3) calls fact(2)  -> Frame fact(2) pushed [n=2]
// Step 3: fact(2) calls fact(1)  -> Frame fact(1) pushed [n=1] (BASE CASE!)
// Stack is now at maximum depth: 3 frames!
ACCUMULATING SUSPENSION
During the winding phase, no multiplications have happened yet! Computations are deferred.
STACK DEPTH = N
The memory consumption of recursive factorial is proportional to N: Space Complexity O(N).
atom 13 · the unwinding phase

THE UNWINDING PHASE — COLLAPSING & COMPUTING

unit4_atom_013.c
/* UNWINDING: Popping frames & evaluating results */
// Step 4: fact(1) returns 1      -> Frame fact(1) popped!
// Step 5: fact(2) computes 2 * 1 = 2 -> Frame fact(2) popped!
// Step 6: fact(3) computes 3 * 2 = 6 -> Frame fact(3) popped!
// Result 6 delivered to main()!
EVALUATION ON THE WAY DOWN
The deferred multiplications `n * fact(n-1)` execute in reverse order as stack frames pop.
CLEAN STACK COLLAPSE
When the unwinding completes, the stack pointer returns to its exact starting position in main().
atom 14 · visual call tree

VISUAL CALL TREES — BOX-TRACE DIAGRAMS

unit4_atom_014.c
/* Box Trace Representation: */
// [fact(3): waiting for fact(2)]
//       └── [fact(2): waiting for fact(1)]
//                 └── [fact(1): returns 1]
//       ┌── [returns 2 * 1 = 2]
// [returns 3 * 2 = 6]
DIAGRAMMING TRACES
Box-tracing or tree diagrams allow engineers to visually audit recursive states on whiteboards or exams.
BRANCHING FACTOR
Linear recursion has a single branch (chain). Tree recursion (like Fibonacci) produces a branching canopy.
atom 15 · trace table construction

RIGOROUS TRACE TABLES — TABULAR STATE AUDIT

unit4_atom_015.c
/* Trace Table for fact(3) */
// Call   Param n   Base?   Recursive Call   Returned Value
// #1     3         No      3 * fact(2)      3 * 2 = 6
// #2     2         No      2 * fact(1)      2 * 1 = 2
// #3     1         YES     None             1
STEPWISE VERIFICATION
Constructing a trace table forces explicit identification of parameter bindings and return flows.
CONFIDENCE IN CORRECTION
Guarantees that off-by-one base cases (e.g. stopping at `n=0` vs `n=1`) are caught before coding.
atom 16 · debugging with indentation

DEBUGGING RECURSION — INDENTATION LOGGING

unit4_atom_016.c
int trace_fact(int n, int depth) {
    for (int i = 0; i < depth; i++) printf("  ");
    printf("ENTER fact(%d)\n", n);
    
    int result;
    if (n <= 1) result = 1;
    else        result = n * trace_fact(n - 1, depth + 1);
    
    for (int i = 0; i < depth; i++) printf("  ");
    printf("LEAVE fact(%d) = %d\n", n, result);
    return result;
}
VISUALIZING STACK DEPTH
Passing a `depth` parameter that increments on each call creates an indented visual tree in console output.
INVALUABLE FOR STUDENTS
Immediately reveals where functions enter, recurse, hit base cases, and return.
atom 17 · call tree explosion

TREE RECURSION — THE BRANCHING CANOPY

unit4_atom_017.c
/* Tree Recursion: Two recursive calls per invocation */
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return 0;
    if (n == 1) return 1;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); // Two branches!
}
EXPONENTIAL GROWTH
Each call spawns TWO more calls. Tree depth N produces 2^N calls! `fib(40)` executes over 1 BILLION calls!
OVERLAPPING SUBPROBLEMS
`fib(3)` is recalculated thousands of times redundantly. A massive performance bottleneck without memoization.
atom 18 · fibonacci call tree

FIBONACCI CALL TREE — VISUALIZING REDUNDANCY

unit4_atom_018.c
/* Call tree for fib(4): */
//                  fib(4)
//               /          \
//          fib(3)            fib(2)
//         /      \          /      \
//     fib(2)    fib(1)   fib(1)   fib(0)
//    /      \
// fib(1)   fib(0)    // Notice fib(2) is solved TWICE!
EXPONENTIAL CANOPY
The tree branches out into a full binary tree of depth N.
DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING MOTIVATION
Seeing this redundant tree is the exact motivation for learning Dynamic Programming and Memoization in advanced algorithms.
atom 19 · converting to iteration

CONVERTING TO LOOPS — REPLACING CALL STACK

unit4_atom_019.c
/* Iterative Factorial: O(1) Memory */
int fact_iter(int n) {
    int result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}
ZERO STACK OVERHEAD
Runs in a single stack frame with O(1) space, never risking stack overflow even for huge numbers.
MECHANICAL TRANSLATION
Tail recursive functions can always be converted to simple while or for loops in 30 seconds.
atom 20 · tracing pitfalls

TRACING PITFALLS — MISSING RETURN VALUE

unit4_atom_020.c
/* FATAL TRACING BUG: Forgetting to return the recursive call! */
int bad_sum(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return 0;
    n + bad_sum(n - 1); // BUG! Missing 'return' keyword!
    // Function drops off the end and returns garbage!
}
THE MISSING RETURN
Crucial bug: writing `sub_function()` without `return sub_function()`. The callee evaluates but the answer is discarded!
COMPILER ASSISTANCE
Flag `-Wreturn-type` catches this immediately. Always return the recursive calculation.
atom 21 · tracing summary

TRACING SUMMARY — MASTERY CHECKLIST

unit4_atom_021.c
/* Tracing Checklist: */
// 1. Winding: Stack grows downward, calls accumulate
// 2. Base Case: Halts growth and initiates reversal
// 3. Unwinding: Stack collapses upward, results compute
// 4. Time: Total nodes in call tree
// 5. Space: Maximum depth of call stack
// Next: Mathematical Recursive Functions!
MENTAL MODEL SOLIDIFIED
You now understand exactly how the hardware execution stack handles recursive call lifecycles.
TRANSITION TO MATH FUNCTIONS
Now we examine classic mathematical algorithms formulated recursively in C.
atom 22 · factorial algorithm

RECURSIVE FACTORIAL — CANONICAL ALGORITHM

unit4_atom_022.c
long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1; /* Base Case: 0! = 1! = 1 */
    return (long long)n * factorial(n - 1); /* n! = n * (n-1)! */
}

int main(void) {
    printf("10! = %lld\n", factorial(10)); // 3628800
    return 0;
}
MATHEMATICAL RECURRENCE
Direct translation of the formal mathematical definition: n! = n * (n-1)! for n > 0.
FAST GROWTH
13! overflows 32-bit signed int (2.1 billion). 21! overflows 64-bit long long. Always check input ranges.
atom 23 · linear power

LINEAR POWER — O(N) RECURSIVE EXPONENT

unit4_atom_023.c
double power_linear(double base, int exp) {
    if (exp == 0) return 1.0; /* Base Case: x^0 = 1 */
    if (exp < 0)  return 1.0 / power_linear(base, -exp);
    
    return base * power_linear(base, exp - 1);
}
HANDLING NEGATIVES
Gracefully handles negative powers by returning `1.0 / x^(-exp)`.
O(N) DEPTH
Takes `exp` stack frames. Can we do better? Yes: Fast Binary Exponentiation!
atom 24 · fast binary power

FAST POWER — O(log N) EXPONENTIATION

unit4_atom_024.c
double power_fast(double base, int exp) {
    if (exp == 0) return 1.0;
    
    double half = power_fast(base, exp / 2); /* Divide and conquer! */
    
    if (exp % 2 == 0) return half * half;         // Even: (x^(n/2))^2
    else             return base * half * half;  // Odd:  x * (x^(n/2))^2
}
LOGARITHMIC SPEEDUP
Computing 2^1024 with linear power takes 1,024 recursive steps. Fast power does it in only 10 steps!
AVOID REDUNDANT CALLS
Store `half` in a variable! Calling `power_fast(base, exp/2) * power_fast(...)` ruins the O(log N) speedup!
atom 25 · euclid gcd

EUCLID'S GCD — GREATEST COMMON DIVISOR

unit4_atom_025.c
/* Euclidean Algorithm: 300 BC */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) return a; /* Base Case: GCD(a, 0) = a */
    return gcd(b, a % b);  /* Recursive Step: GCD(b, a mod b) */
}

int main(void) {
    printf("GCD(48, 18) = %d\n", gcd(48, 18)); // 6
    return 0;
}
TIMELESS BEAUTY
One of the oldest and most elegant algorithms in human civilization. Operates in logarithmic time O(log(min(a, b))).
AUTOMATIC ORDERING
If `a < b`, the first step `a % b` automatically swaps them: `gcd(18, 48 % 18) -> gcd(18, 12)`.
atom 26 · lcm via gcd

LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE — LCM VIA RECURSIVE GCD

unit4_atom_026.c
int lcm(int a, int b) {
    if (a == 0 || b == 0) return 0;
    /* LCM(a, b) = (|a * b|) / GCD(a, b) */
    return (a / gcd(a, b)) * b; /* Divide first to prevent overflow! */
}
COMPOSING RECURSIVE MODULES
Reuses the recursive `gcd()` function directly to solve Least Common Multiple.
OVERFLOW PREVENTION
Notice `(a / gcd(a, b)) * b`: Dividing before multiplying prevents intermediate integer overflow!
atom 27 · sum of natural numbers

SUM OF NUMBERS — TRIANGULAR NUMBERS

unit4_atom_027.c
int sum_natural(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return n + sum_natural(n - 1);
}
// sum_natural(5) = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 = n*(n+1)/2
GAUSSIAN EQUIVALENCE
Computes the sum of integers 1 to N recursively. Equivalent to Gauss's formula `n*(n+1)/2`.
INDUCTIVE VERIFICATION
Base case `n=1` returns 1. Step assumes `sum(n-1)` is correct and adds `n`.
atom 28 · sum of digits

SUM OF DIGITS — MODULO RECURSION

unit4_atom_028.c
int sum_digits(int n) {
    if (n < 10) return n; /* Base Case: Single digit */
    return (n % 10) + sum_digits(n / 10); /* Last digit + rest */
}

// sum_digits(4096) -> 6 + sum_digits(409) -> 6 + 9 + 0 + 4 = 19
NUMBER PEELING
`n % 10` extracts the rightmost digit; `n / 10` passes the remaining truncated integer to the recursive call.
NATURAL TERMINATION
When `n < 10`, only one digit remains, halting recursion naturally without string conversion.
atom 29 · decimal to binary

DECIMAL TO BINARY — REVERSAL ON UNWINDING

unit4_atom_029.c
void print_binary(unsigned int n) {
    if (n > 1) {
        print_binary(n / 2); /* Recurse on higher bits FIRST */
    }
    printf("%u", n % 2);     /* Prints on unwinding (Lowest bits last) */
}

// print_binary(13) prints "1101"
AUTOMATIC REVERSAL
Normally, modulo division generates bits in reverse order. By recursing BEFORE printing, the stack prints in correct order!
ZERO BUFFER NEEDED
Eliminates the need to store bits in a temporary array or reverse a string.
atom 30 · tower of hanoi rules

TOWER OF HANOI — THE CLASSIC PUZZLE

unit4_atom_030.c
/* The Tower of Hanoi Rules: */
// 3 Pegs: Source (A), Target (C), Auxiliary (B)
// N Disks stacked in decreasing size on Peg A
// Objective: Move all N disks from A to C
// Rule 1: Move only ONE disk at a time
// Rule 2: Never place a LARGER disk on top of a SMALLER disk!
LEGENDARY PUZZLE
Invented by Édouard Lucas in 1883. An impossible puzzle for iterative code, but solved in 4 lines of recursive C!
REDUCTION STRATEGY
To move N disks from A to C: (1) Move N-1 to B, (2) Move disk N to C, (3) Move N-1 from B to C.
atom 31 · tower of hanoi algorithm

HANOI ALGORITHM — THE 4-LINE SOLUTION

unit4_atom_031.c
void hanoi(int n, char from, char to, char aux) {
    if (n == 1) {
        printf("Move disk 1 from %c -> %c\n", from, to);
        return;
    }
    hanoi(n - 1, from, aux, to); /* Step 1: Move N-1 from -> aux */
    printf("Move disk %d from %c -> %c\n", n, from, to); /* Step 2 */
    hanoi(n - 1, aux, to, from); /* Step 3: Move N-1 aux -> to */
}
RECURSIVE DECOMPOSITION
Notice how the roles of the pegs switch! In Step 1, `aux` acts as the target. In Step 3, `aux` acts as the source.
EXPONENTIAL MOVES: 2^N - 1
Moving 3 disks takes 7 moves. Moving 64 disks takes 18 quintillion moves (584 billion years!).
atom 32 · hanoi trace 3 disks

HANOI TRACE: 3 DISKS — COMPLETE MOVE SEQUENCE

unit4_atom_032.c
/* Output of hanoi(3, 'A', 'C', 'B'): */
// Move disk 1 from A -> C
// Move disk 2 from A -> B
// Move disk 1 from C -> B
// Move disk 3 from A -> C  <-- Largest disk placed on target!
// Move disk 1 from B -> A
// Move disk 2 from B -> C
// Move disk 1 from A -> C  <-- Complete! (7 moves)
SYMMETRICAL BEAUTY
Disk 1 moves on every second step. Notice the perfect fractal symmetry of the move pattern.
OPTIMAL SOLUTION
Mathematics proves that 2^N - 1 is the absolute minimum possible number of moves to solve Hanoi.
atom 33 · memoization preview

MEMOIZATION PREVIEW — CACHING FIBONACCI

unit4_atom_033.c
long long memo[100] = {0};

long long fib_memo(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    if (memo[n] != 0) return memo[n]; /* Cache hit! O(1) return */
    
    memo[n] = fib_memo(n - 1) + fib_memo(n - 2); /* Cache write */
    return memo[n];
}
// Turns O(2^N) exponential catastrophe into lightning-fast O(N)!
CACHE LOOKUP
Before computing, check if the answer is already stored in an array. If present, return it immediately.
DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING
Memoization bridges pure mathematical recursion with high-performance linear algorithms.
atom 34 · math recursion summary

MATH RECURSION SUMMARY — PATTERNS CATALOG

unit4_atom_034.c
/* Mathematical Recursion Mastered: */
// 1. Factorial & Exponentiation: Linear decomposition
// 2. Fast Power: Binary logarithmic split O(log N)
// 3. Euclid GCD: Remainder reduction
// 4. Tower of Hanoi: Multi-peg divide and conquer
// Next: Recursion with Arrays and Strings!
ALGORITHMIC POWER
Mathematical recurrence relations map with 1:1 clarity into C recursive functions.
TRANSITION TO ARRAYS & STRINGS
Now we apply recursion to data structures: traversing arrays and strings recursively.
atom 35 · recursive array concept

RECURSIVE ARRAYS — HEAD AND TAIL THINKING

unit4_atom_035.c
/* Array as Head and Tail: */
// Array: [ 10, 20, 30, 40 ]
// Head:  10 (First element, arr[0])
// Tail:  [ 20, 30, 40 ] (Subarray of size N-1 starting at arr+1)

// Any array problem can be reduced to: Operate on Head + Recurse on Tail!
HEAD AND TAIL IDIOM
The foundational pattern for processing collections recursively. Common in functional languages (Lisp, Haskell, Erlang).
POINTER PROGRESSION
In C, the tail is simply `arr + 1` with size `size - 1`. Zero copying required!
atom 36 · recursive array sum

RECURSIVE ARRAY SUM — ACCUMULATION ON UNWINDING

unit4_atom_036.c
int recursive_sum(const int arr[], int size) {
    if (size == 0) return 0; /* Base Case: Empty array sum is 0 */
    
    return arr[0] + recursive_sum(arr + 1, size - 1); /* Head + Tail */
}

// recursive_sum({5, 10, 15}, 3) -> 5 + (10 + (15 + 0)) = 30
ELEGANT SUMMATION
Combines the head element with the recursively computed sum of the remaining tail elements.
O(N) STACK DEPTH
Traverses the array element-by-element, unwinding from the empty base case.
atom 37 · recursive array max

RECURSIVE ARRAY MAX — FINDING EXTREMA

unit4_atom_037.c
int recursive_max(const int arr[], int size) {
    if (size == 1) return arr[0]; /* Base Case: Single element */
    
    int max_of_tail = recursive_max(arr + 1, size - 1);
    return (arr[0] > max_of_tail) ? arr[0] : max_of_tail;
}
INDIVIDUAL COMPARISON
Finds the maximum of the tail subarray and compares it against the head element.
GUARD AGAINST EMPTY
Assumes `size >= 1`. An array of size 1 trivially has its sole element as maximum.
atom 38 · recursive linear search

RECURSIVE LINEAR SEARCH — SEQUENTIAL MATCHING

unit4_atom_038.c
int rec_linear_search(const int arr[], int size, int target) {
    if (size == 0) return -1;             // Base 1: Not found
    if (arr[0] == target) return 0;       // Base 2: Found at head!
    
    int sub_idx = rec_linear_search(arr + 1, size - 1, target);
    if (sub_idx == -1) return -1;
    return 1 + sub_idx; /* Adjust index offset! */
}
TWO BASE CASES
Recursion terminates either when the target is found at the head, or when the array is exhausted (`size == 0`).
INDEX OFFSET ADJUSTMENT
Notice `1 + sub_idx`: Accounts for the fact that the tail starts one index higher than the original array.
atom 39 · recursive binary search

RECURSIVE BINARY SEARCH — DIVIDE & CONQUER

unit4_atom_039.c
int rec_bin_search(const int arr[], int low, int high, int target) {
    if (low > high) return -1; /* Base Case: Exhausted */
    
    int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
    if (arr[mid] == target)      return mid;
    else if (arr[mid] > target)  return rec_bin_search(arr, low, mid - 1, target);
    else                         return rec_bin_search(arr, mid + 1, high, target);
}
NATURAL FIT FOR RECURSION
Binary search is inherently divide-and-conquer. Recursion models it with supreme mathematical elegance.
O(log N) STACK DEPTH
Even for an array of 1,000,000 items, the recursive stack never exceeds 20 frames!
atom 40 · recursive string length

RECURSIVE STRLEN — NULL TERMINATOR ANCHOR

unit4_atom_040.c
size_t rec_strlen(const char *str) {
    if (*str == '\0') return 0; /* Base Case: Hit null terminator */
    return 1 + rec_strlen(str + 1); /* 1 char + length of tail */
}

// rec_strlen("CAT") -> 1 + (1 + (1 + 0)) = 3
NULL TERMINATOR BASE
No explicit `size` parameter needed! The standard C null terminator `\0` acts as the natural stopping condition.
TAIL ADVANCE
`str + 1` advances the pointer to the next character until hitting zero.
atom 41 · recursive string reverse

REVERSING STRINGS — UNWINDING PRINTING

unit4_atom_041.c
void print_reverse(const char *str) {
    if (*str == '\0') return;
    print_reverse(str + 1); /* Recurse to the very end first! */
    putchar(*str);          /* Prints on the way back! */
}

// print_reverse("EMIT") prints "TIME"
HEAD RECURSION POWER
By recursing all the way to `\0` before calling `putchar()`, characters print in reverse order automatically.
ZERO MEMORY ALLOCATION
Reverses text output without allocating a second string buffer in memory.
atom 42 · recursive palindrome

RECURSIVE PALINDROME — EDGE MATCHING

unit4_atom_042.c
int is_palindrome_rec(const char *str, int left, int right) {
    if (left >= right) return 1; /* Base Case: Pointers crossed */
    if (str[left] != str[right]) return 0; /* Mismatch! */
    
    return is_palindrome_rec(str, left + 1, right - 1); /* Recurse inner */
}
BOUNDARY COMPARISON
Tests outer pair of characters. If they match, it recurses inward on the smaller nested substring.
EARLY TERMINATION
Instantly aborts and returns 0 on the first mismatched pair.
atom 43 · recursive count char

COUNTING CHARACTERS — TARGET FILTERING

unit4_atom_043.c
int count_char(const char *str, char target) {
    if (*str == '\0') return 0;
    int match = (*str == target) ? 1 : 0;
    return match + count_char(str + 1, target);
}
COUNTING PREDICATE
Calculates 1 or 0 for the current character, adds it to the recursive count of the tail.
STRING PROCESSING
Demonstrates how text inspection routines operate recursively on character streams.
atom 44 · tail recursion optimization

TAIL CALL OPTIMIZATION — TCO IN GCC / CLANG

unit4_atom_044.c
/* Tail-Recursive Factorial using ACCUMULATOR: */
long long fact_tco(int n, long long acc) {
    if (n <= 1) return acc;
    return fact_tco(n - 1, n * acc); /* PURE TAIL CALL! */
}
// Caller: fact_tco(5, 1); // Returns 120
ACCUMULATOR TECHNIQUE
By passing intermediate results forward in parameter `acc`, no calculation is needed on unwinding.
STACK REUSE (TCO)
Compilers with `-O2` reuse the SAME stack frame! Tail-recursive functions run with O(1) space, identical to while-loops!
atom 45 · array recursion pitfalls

ARRAY RECURSION TRAPS — OFF-BY-ONE POINTERS

unit4_atom_045.c
/* PITFALL: Modifying array inside head recursion */
void bad_rec(int *a, int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return;
    bad_rec(a + 1, n - 1);
    // a[0] = 0; // Caution: Modifies during unwinding in reverse order!
}
POINTER ALIGNMENT
Ensure `a + 1` stays within allocated bounds. Check `size <= 0` base case first.
STACK DEPTH LIMITS
Never use naive recursion on arrays of 1,000,000 elements unless compiled with verified TCO.

atom 47 · struct introduction

USER-DEFINED STRUCTURES — THE STRUCT KEYWORD

unit4_atom_047.c
/* Grouping heterogeneous data into a single type */
struct Student {
    int    id;
    char   name[50];
    double gpa;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student s1; /* Declaring a structure variable */
    s1.id = 101;
    s1.gpa = 3.85;
    return 0;
}
HETEROGENEOUS BUNDLING
Unlike arrays (which hold elements of the SAME type), a `struct` bundles multiple variables of DIFFERENT types into one record.
THE STRUCT TEMPLATE
`struct Student { ... };` is a blueprint. It creates a new type template but allocates no memory until a variable is declared.
atom 48 · member access operator

THE DOT OPERATOR (.) — DIRECT MEMBER ACCESS

unit4_atom_048.c
struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
};

struct Point p1;
p1.x = 10; /* Member access with dot operator */
p1.y = 20;

printf("Coordinates: (%d, %d)\n", p1.x, p1.y);
DIRECT MEMBER ACCESS
The dot operator `.` selects a specific member field within a structure variable.
LVALUE PROPERTY
`p1.x` is a full lvalue: it can be read from, assigned to, or have its address taken (`&p1.x`).
atom 49 · struct initialization

STRUCT INITIALIZATION — POSITIONAL LISTS

unit4_atom_049.c
struct Book {
    char title[40];
    char author[30];
    int  pages;
    double price;
};

/* Positional initialization list */
struct Book b1 = {"The C Programming Language", "K&R", 272, 45.50};
POSITIONAL BINDING
Values in `{ ... }` match structure member fields in the exact order they were declared in the struct template.
ZERO PADDING
If fewer initializers are provided than fields, remaining members are automatically zeroed by C.
atom 50 · designated struct initializers

DESIGNATED INITIALIZERS — C99 NAMED FIELDS

unit4_atom_050.c
/* C99 Designated Initializer for Structs: */
struct Book b2 = {
    .title = "Clean Architecture",
    .price = 39.99,
    .pages = 400
    /* .author is omitted: automatically zeroed! */
};
FIELD-BY-NAME
The `.member = value` syntax allows initializing fields in any arbitrary order by name.
SELF-DOCUMENTING CODE
Eliminates errors caused by misremembering the order of parameters in large structures with 15+ fields.
atom 51 · struct assignment

STRUCT ASSIGNMENT — SHALLOW MEMORY COPY

unit4_atom_051.c
struct Point p1 = {10, 20};
struct Point p2;

p2 = p1; /* LEGAL! Copies ALL bytes from p1 into p2! */

printf("p2: (%d, %d)\n", p2.x, p2.y); // (10, 20)
p2.x = 99; // Modifies p2 ONLY! p1.x is still 10!
WHOLE STRUCT COPY
Unlike arrays, structures CAN be directly assigned using `=`! C executes a fast bitwise copy (`memcpy`) of all internal bytes.
INDEPENDENT INSTANCES
`p2` is a distinct clone in its own memory cells. Modifying `p2` does not affect `p1`.
atom 52 · struct comparison limitation

STRUCT COMPARISON TRAP — NO == OPERATOR

unit4_atom_052.c
struct Point p1 = {1, 2}, p2 = {1, 2};

// if (p1 == p2) // COMPILE ERROR! C does NOT support == on structs!

/* Solution: Write a dedicated equality function */
int points_equal(struct Point a, struct Point b) {
    return (a.x == b.x && a.y == b.y);
}
WHY == IS ILLEGAL
Structs often contain invisible padding bytes filled with garbage memory. A raw byte comparison would fail even if member values match!
CUSTOM EQUALITY FUNCTIONS
Always author explicit member-by-member comparison functions when testing structure equivalence.
atom 53 · typedef idiom

THE TYPEDEF IDIOM — CLEAN TYPE ALIASES

unit4_atom_053.c
/* Without typedef: must write 'struct Student' everywhere */
struct Student s1;

/* With typedef: create clean first-class type name */
typedef struct {
    int id;
    double gpa;
} Student;

Student s2; /* Clean syntax, identical to primitive types! */
ELIMINATING STRUCT KEYWORD
`typedef` defines a type alias. `Student s2;` reads cleanly without cluttering code with the `struct` keyword.
CANONICAL C IDIOM
Virtually all major production C codebases (Linux, SQLite, Git) use typedef for struct definitions.
atom 54 · named vs anonymous structs

TAG NAMES & TYPEDEF — SELF-REFERENTIAL TYPES

unit4_atom_054.c
/* Both tag name AND typedef alias: */
typedef struct Node {
    int data;
    struct Node *next; /* MUST use 'struct Node' here! */
} Node;

Node n1; // Typedef used for variable declaration
SELF-REFERENTIAL TAG
Inside the struct body, the typedef alias `Node` is not defined yet! You must provide a tag name `struct Node` for internal pointers.
DUAL CONVENTION
`typedef struct Tag { ... } Alias;` provides the best of both worlds.
atom 55 · memory layout of structs

STRUCT MEMORY MAP — CONSECUTIVE ALLOCATION

unit4_atom_055.c
/* Consecutive member storage */
typedef struct {
    int a;    // 4 bytes
    int b;    // 4 bytes
    double c; // 8 bytes
} Sample;

// Total theoretical bytes = 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes
MEMBER ORDER PRESERVED
C guarantees that members are laid out in memory in the exact order they are declared in the struct template.
ADDRESS ORDER
Address of `a` < Address of `b` < Address of `c`. `&sample.a` equals the base address of the entire struct.
atom 56 · struct memory size

STRUCT SIZEOF — TOTAL ALLOCATION

unit4_atom_056.c
typedef struct {
    char c;
    int i;
} Example;

printf("sizeof(Example) = %zu bytes\n", sizeof(Example));
// Expected: 1 + 4 = 5 bytes?
// ACTUAL ON 64-BIT: 8 bytes! (3 padding bytes added!)
THE SIZEOF SURPRISE
The size of a struct is often GREATER than the sum of its individual member sizes!
ALIGNMENT REQUIREMENT
CPUs require data types to align on natural memory boundaries. This leads directly to Structure Padding!
atom 57 · alignment and padding intro

MEMORY ALIGNMENT — HARDWARE BUS EFFICIENCY

unit4_atom_057.c
/* CPU Word Boundaries */
// 32-bit CPU reads RAM in 4-byte chunks
// 64-bit CPU reads RAM in 8-byte chunks
// Placing a 4-byte int at an odd address (e.g. 0x101) forces
// the CPU to execute TWO bus reads and bit-shifts!
HARDWARE ALIGNMENT RULES
`char` aligns on 1-byte boundary. `short` aligns on 2-byte boundary. `int` aligns on 4-byte boundary. `double` aligns on 8-byte boundary.
COMPILER INTERVENTION
To maximize execution speed, compilers insert invisible "padding bytes" between members to satisfy alignment rules.
atom 58 · member reordering

MEMBER REORDERING — OPTIMIZING STRUCT SIZE

unit4_atom_058.c
/* POOR ORDER: 24 Bytes (Lots of padding!) */
struct Bad  { char a; double b; int c; };

/* OPTIMIZED ORDER: 16 Bytes (8 bytes saved!) */
struct Good { double b; int c; char a; };
LARGEST TO SMALLEST
Rule of thumb: Order struct members from largest to smallest type (`double` -> `int` -> `short` -> `char`).
EMBEDDED SAVINGS
In an array of 1,000,000 structs, saving 8 bytes per struct recovers 8 Megabytes of RAM instantly!
atom 59 · offsetof macro

THE OFFSETOF MACRO — INSPECTION

unit4_atom_059.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stddef.h>

struct Record {
    char tag;
    int id;
    double score;
};

printf("Offset of tag:   %zu\n", offsetof(struct Record, tag));   // 0
printf("Offset of id:    %zu\n", offsetof(struct Record, id));    // 4 (3 pad bytes!)
printf("Offset of score: %zu\n", offsetof(struct Record, score)); // 8
BYTE OFFSET QUERY
`offsetof(type, member)` computes the exact byte distance of a member from the start of the struct at compile time.
SYSTEM AUDITING
Essential for binary file parsing, device drivers, and network protocol serializers.
atom 60 · passing struct by value

PASSING BY VALUE — FULL STRUCT COPY

unit4_atom_060.c
typedef struct { double x, y; } Point;

void display_point(Point p) { /* Passed by VALUE */
    printf("(%.1f, %.1f)\n", p.x, p.y);
    p.x = 0; // Modifies local copy only! Caller unaffected!
}
CALL-BY-VALUE COPY
Passing a struct by value copies every single member byte-for-byte onto the callee stack frame.
SAFE BUT EXPENSIVE
For small structs (like Point: 16 bytes), passing by value is clean, safe, and modern.
atom 61 · performance bottleneck

COPY BOTTLENECK — LARGE STRUCT PASSING

unit4_atom_061.c
typedef struct {
    char buffer[4096]; // 4 KB of data!
    int status;
} BigData;

// void process(BigData b); // SLOW! Copies 4,100 bytes on every call!
// void process(const BigData *b); // FAST! Copies only 8 bytes!
STACK OVERHEAD
Passing large structures by value wastes CPU cycles copying thousands of bytes and risks Stack Overflow.
PASSING BY POINTER
Passing a pointer to the struct copies a single 8-byte address regardless of struct size. O(1) performance!
atom 62 · passing struct by pointer

PASSING BY POINTER — THE DEREFERENCE TRAP

unit4_atom_062.c
void translate(Point *p, double dx, double dy) {
    /* Clunky notation: (*p).member */
    (*p).x += dx; /* Parentheses MANDATORY because . beats * ! */
    (*p).y += dy;
}
PRECEDENCE PROBLEM
The dot operator `.` has higher precedence than the dereference operator `*`. Writing `*p.x` means `*(p.x)`, which causes a compiler error!
MANDATORY PARENS
You must write `(*p).x` to dereference first, then access the member. But C provides a much cleaner solution: The Arrow Operator!
atom 63 · the arrow operator

THE ARROW OPERATOR (->) — DEREFERENCE + ACCESS

unit4_atom_063.c
/* Syntactic Sugar: p->member IS IDENTICAL TO (*p).member */
void translate_clean(Point *p, double dx, double dy) {
    p->x += dx;
    p->y += dy;
}

int main(void) {
    Point pt = {10.0, 20.0};
    translate_clean(&pt, 5.0, -2.0); // Pass address with &
    printf("pt: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", pt.x, pt.y); // (15.0, 18.0)
    return 0;
}
THE -> OPERATOR
Combines pointer dereferencing and member access into a single clean token: `ptr->field`.
GOLDEN RULE
Use the DOT `.` on actual struct variables. Use the ARROW `->` on pointers to struct variables!
atom 64 · const struct pointers

CONST STRUCT POINTERS — READ-ONLY EFFICIENCY

unit4_atom_064.c
/* Fast 8-byte passing + Immutability Guarantee */
void print_student(const Student *s) {
    printf("ID: %d, GPA: %.2f\n", s->id, s->gpa);
    // s->gpa = 4.0; // COMPILE ERROR: Assignment of read-only member!
}
THE INDUSTRY STANDARD
Combining `const` with pointer passing gives you the zero-overhead speed of pointers with the safety of pass-by-value.
API DESIGN CONTRACT
Always declare input-only struct pointers as `const Type *ptr`.

atom 76 · sorting array of structs

SORTING RECORDS — SWAPPING FULL STRUCTS

unit4_atom_076.c
void sort_by_gpa(Student arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (arr[j].gpa < arr[j + 1].gpa) { // Descending
                Student temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp; /* Swaps ENTIRE student record! */
            }
        }
    }
}
SYNCHRONIZED SWAPS
Because `arr[j]` is a struct, `Student temp = arr[j]` swaps ID, GPA, name, and all fields together!
ZERO DESYNCHRONIZATION
Solves the fatal flaw of parallel arrays. Data integrity is guaranteed 100%.

/* In-Memory Data Models Complete: */
// 1. Single struct = One record (Row)
// 2. Array of structs = Entire database table

Every database management system (DBMS) stores rows internally as structured records.
TRANSITION TO UNIONS
Now we examine a special C construct that shares memory: The Union.
atom 80 · union introduction

UNION TYPES — SHARED MEMORY ALLOCATION

unit4_atom_080.c
/* Union: Members share the EXACT SAME starting memory address! */
union Data {
    int    i; // 4 bytes
    float  f; // 4 bytes
    char   c; // 1 byte
};

union Data d;
printf("sizeof(d) = %zu bytes\n", sizeof(d)); // Exactly 4 bytes!
SHARED MEMORY STORAGE
Unlike a struct (where members sit side-by-side), in a union, all members overlap at byte offset 0!
SIZE OF UNION
The size of a union equals the size of its LARGEST member (plus alignment padding if necessary).
atom 81 · union overwrite behavior

MEMBER OVERWRITE — ONE ACTIVE VALUE AT A TIME

unit4_atom_081.c
union Data d;
d.i = 42;
printf("d.i = %d\n", d.i); // 42

d.f = 3.14f; /* Overwrites the bytes of d.i! */
printf("d.f = %.2f\n", d.f); // 3.14
printf("d.i is now CORRUPTED: %d\n", d.i); // Garbage integer!
MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE
A union can hold only ONE valid member value at any given time. Assigning one member overwrites the others.
SPACE SAVING
Used when an entity can be an Integer OR a Float OR a String, but never more than one simultaneously.
atom 82 · type punning

TYPE PUNNING — LOW-LEVEL BIT INSPECTION

unit4_atom_082.c
/* Inspecting the raw IEEE-754 binary bits of a float */
union FloatInspector {
    float f;
    unsigned int bits;
};

union FloatInspector fi;
fi.f = -1.0f;
printf("Hex bits of -1.0: 0x%08X\n", fi.bits); // 0xBF800000
TYPE PUNNING
Reading the bytes of one type through the lens of another type without performing a numerical conversion.
SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING
Used in hardware drivers, network serialization, and fast mathematical algorithms (like Quake's fast inverse square root).
atom 83 · tagged unions concept

TAGGED UNIONS — SAFE VARIANT TYPES

unit4_atom_083.c
/* Combining an enum tag with a union inside a struct */
enum ValueType { TYPE_INT, TYPE_FLOAT, TYPE_STRING };

typedef struct {
    enum ValueType type; /* Discriminator Tag */
    union {
        int   i_val;
        float f_val;
        char  s_val[20];
    } data;
} VariantValue;
DISCRIMINATED UNIONS
The enum `type` tells the program WHICH member of the union currently contains valid data.
FOUNDATION OF DYNAMIC TYPES
How dynamically typed languages (Python, JavaScript) represent arbitrary variable values in C!

PROCESSING VARIANTS — SWITCH-CASE DISPATCH

unit4_atom_084.c
void print_variant(const VariantValue *v) {
    switch (v->type) {
        case TYPE_INT:    printf("Int: %d\n", v->data.i_val); break;
        case TYPE_FLOAT:  printf("Float: %.2f\n", v->data.f_val); break;
        case TYPE_STRING: printf("String: %s\n", v->data.s_val); break;
    }
}
TYPE-SAFE ACCESS
The switch-case statement inspects the tag before reading the union, guaranteeing the program never reads corrupted memory.

Adding a new supported type simply requires adding an enum constant and a new union field.
atom 85 · bit fields syntax

BIT-FIELDS — PACKING HARDWARE FLAGS

unit4_atom_085.c
/* Pack multiple boolean flags into single bits */
typedef struct {
    unsigned int is_admin    : 1; /* 1 bit wide (0 or 1) */
    unsigned int is_verified : 1; /* 1 bit wide */
    unsigned int theme_color : 4; /* 4 bits wide (0 to 15) */
    unsigned int security_lvl: 2; /* 2 bits wide (0 to 3) */
} UserPermissions;
// Total size = 4 bytes (packs 8 distinct attributes into 1 word!)
BIT-LEVEL PRECISION
Syntax `type member : width;` tells the compiler to allocate exactly that number of bits.
HARDWARE REGISTERS
Used universally in microcontrollers, embedded drivers, and network headers to match exact hardware bit specifications.
atom 86 · bit fields restrictions

BIT-FIELD RESTRICTIONS — NO & OPERATOR

unit4_atom_086.c
UserPermissions perm = {1, 1, 12, 3};

// printf("%p", &perm.is_admin); // COMPILE ERROR: Cannot take address of bit-field!
// Addresses in computer RAM exist ONLY for full BYTES, not individual bits!
NO ADDRESS-OF (&)
CPUs address bytes, not bits. Taking the address of a bit-field is illegal in C grammar.
PORTABILITY CAVEAT
Whether bit-fields are allocated left-to-right (little endian) or right-to-left (big endian) is compiler-dependent.
atom 87 · self referential structs

SELF-REFERENTIAL STRUCTS — POINTERS TO SELF

unit4_atom_087.c
/* A struct containing a pointer to its own type! */
typedef struct Node {
    int data;
    struct Node *next; /* Pointer to next Node */
} Node;

Node n1 = {10, NULL};

n1.next = &n2; /* Linked List connection! */

Pointers to identical struct types form the foundation of dynamic data structures: Linked Lists, Trees, and Graphs.
CANNOT EMBED VALUE
Writing `struct Node next;` (without pointer `*`) is illegal: infinite recursive size! It MUST be a pointer `*next`.
atom 88 · linked chain traversal

LINKED TRAVERSAL — WALKING THE POINTERS

unit4_atom_088.c
void print_list(const Node *head) {
    const Node *curr = head;
    while (curr != NULL) {
        printf("%d -> ", curr->data);
        curr = curr->next; /* Advance pointer to next node */
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}
// Output: 10 -> 20 -> NULL
POINTER CHASING
Follows the chain of addresses in memory until encountering the sentinel `NULL` pointer.
DYNAMIC FLEXIBILITY
Nodes can be inserted or deleted anywhere in O(1) time without shifting elements like arrays.
atom 89 · tree traversal preview

TREE TRAVERSAL — IN-ORDER & PRE-ORDER

unit4_atom_089.c
/* Recursive Binary Tree Node */
typedef struct TreeNode {
    int val;
    struct TreeNode *left;
    struct TreeNode *right;
} TreeNode;

void print_in_order(const TreeNode *root) {
    if (root == NULL) return;
    print_in_order(root->left);  /* 1. Visit left subtree */
    printf("%d ", root->val);    /* 2. Process root */
    print_in_order(root->right); /* 3. Visit right subtree */
}
NATURAL RECURSIVE MAPPING
Tree traversal is virtually impossible to write cleanly without recursion. Recursion mirrors the recursive definition of trees.
IN-ORDER SORTING
For a Binary Search Tree (BST), in-order traversal outputs all elements in perfectly sorted ascending order!
atom 90 · tail recursive string

TAIL-RECURSIVE STRINGS — ACCUMULATOR BUFFER

unit4_atom_090.c
void rev_tail(const char *src, char *dest, int len, int idx) {
    if (idx >= len) {
        dest[idx] = '\0';
        return;
    }
    dest[idx] = src[len - 1 - idx];
    rev_tail(src, dest, len, idx + 1); /* Tail call */
}
BUFFER ACCUMULATION
Writes reversed characters directly into destination buffer during the winding phase.
COMPILER ZERO STACK
Executed with zero stack overhead when compiled with optimization flags.

atom 93 · selection sort structs

SORTING STRUCTS — SELECTION SORT ON KEY

unit4_atom_093.c
void sort_students_by_id(Student arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int min_idx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (arr[j].id < arr[min_idx].id) min_idx = j;
        }
        Student temp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[min_idx];
        arr[min_idx] = temp;
    }
}

Compares the primary key `id`, but swaps the entire multi-field struct entity.
MINIMAL WRITES
Performs at most N-1 struct copy operations, maximizing cache efficiency.
atom 94 · binary search structs

BINARY SEARCH STRUCTS — O(LOG N) RECORD LOOKUP

unit4_atom_094.c
int search_student_id(const Student arr[], int n, int target_id) {
    int low = 0, high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (arr[mid].id == target_id)      return mid; // Match!
        else if (arr[mid].id < target_id)  low = mid + 1;
        else                               high = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
RECORD LOOKUP SPEED
Searches 100,000 student records in memory in under 17 comparisons!
PRECONDITION REQUIREMENT
The struct array must be pre-sorted by the target lookup field before binary searching.
