atom 01 · persistence concept

FILE PERSISTENCE — VOLATILE RAM vs DISK

unit5_atom_001.c
/* Why Files? Variables in RAM vanish when power turns off! */
// RAM: High speed, volatile, limited capacity (16 GB)
// Disk / SSD: Persistent, non-volatile, large capacity (1 TB)

// Files allow C programs to save and reload state across runs.
PERSISTENCE GUARANTEE
Files store data permanently on secondary storage (hard drive, SSD, NVMe, USB) until explicitly deleted.
THE STREAM MODEL
In C and Unix, a file is treated as a uniform continuous stream of bytes.
atom 02 · stream abstraction

THE STREAM ABSTRACTION — THE FILE* HANDLE

unit5_atom_002.c
#include <stdio.h>

/* The FILE structure control block: */
FILE *fp; /* Pointer to an opaque FILE stream structure */

// Tracks: (1) Current byte position, (2) Buffer pointer,
//         (3) Error status flags, (4) File descriptor integer
OPAQUE HANDLE
You never manipulate `FILE` members directly; you pass the pointer `FILE *fp` to standard library functions.
STANDARD STREAMS
C automatically opens 3 streams at launch: `stdin` (keyboard, 0), `stdout` (screen, 1), `stderr` (errors, 2).
atom 03 · file opening modes

FILE MODES — READ, WRITE & APPEND

unit5_atom_003.c
/* fopen(filename, mode) */
FILE *f1 = fopen("data.txt", "r"); /* READ: Must already exist! */
FILE *f2 = fopen("out.txt",  "w"); /* WRITE: Truncates / creates! */
FILE *f3 = fopen("log.txt",  "a"); /* APPEND: Writes at end! */
"r" (READ)
Fails (returns NULL) if the file does not exist. The file position indicator is set to byte 0.
"w" (WRITE)
If file exists, IT IS INSTANTLY OVERWRITTEN (TRUNCATED TO 0 BYTES)! If absent, creates a new file. Use caution!
atom 04 · extended update modes

EXTENDED MODES — READ & WRITE (+)

unit5_atom_004.c
/* Extended Update Modes */
FILE *fp1 = fopen("db.txt", "r+"); /* Open for both reading & writing */
FILE *fp2 = fopen("db.txt", "w+"); /* Truncate, open for read & write */
FILE *fp3 = fopen("db.txt", "a+"); /* Open for read & append */
"r+" (READ/UPDATE)
Allows both reading and writing without destroying existing content. Starts at beginning of file.
"a+" (APPEND/UPDATE)
Reads anywhere via `fseek()`, but ALL writes are forced by OS to the very end of file.
atom 05 · mandatory null check

OPENING VERIFICATION — THE MANDATORY NULL CHECK

unit5_atom_005.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    FILE *fp = fopen("missing_file.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        perror("[ERROR] Failed to open file");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE); /* Abort execution cleanly! */
    }
    // Safe to proceed with file operations
    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}
MANDATORY NULL CHECK
`fopen()` returns NULL if the file does not exist, disk is full, or permission is denied. Dereferencing NULL crashes!
PERROR() UTILITY
`perror("msg")` prints your message followed by the operating system's exact reason (e.g. "No such file or directory").
atom 06 · closing files

CLOSING FILES — FCLOSE & FLUSHING

unit5_atom_006.c
/* Always close opened files! */
int result = fclose(fp);
if (result != 0) {
    perror("Error closing file");
}
// fp = NULL; // Safe defensive practice
FLUSHING WRITE BUFFERS
Operating systems buffer file writes in RAM for speed. `fclose()` guarantees all buffered bytes are physically flushed to disk.
RESOURCE LEAKAGE
The OS limits open file descriptors (typically 1024). Forgetting `fclose()` exhausts file handles, crashing servers.
atom 07 · character file io

CHARACTER FILE I/O — FGETC & FPUTC

unit5_atom_007.c
/* fgetc returns INT, not char, to represent EOF (-1)! */
int ch;
FILE *src = fopen("source.txt", "r");

while ((ch = fgetc(src)) != EOF) {
    putchar(ch); // Echo character to console
}
fclose(src);
WHY INT FOR FGETC?
A `char` holds 0 to 255. `EOF` is typically `-1`. An 8-bit char cannot distinguish between byte 255 and EOF! `int` is strictly required.
BYTE-BY-BYTE STREAM
Reads raw characters sequentially, preserving all spaces, tabs, and newlines.
atom 08 · file copy utility

FILE COPY UTILITY — COMPLETE C PROGRAM

unit5_atom_008.c
#include <stdio.h>

int copy_file(const char *src_name, const char *dest_name) {
    FILE *in = fopen(src_name, "rb");
    if (!in) return 0;
    FILE *out = fopen(dest_name, "wb");
    if (!out) { fclose(in); return 0; }
    
    int c;
    while ((c = fgetc(in)) != EOF) {
        fputc(c, out);
    }
    fclose(in); fclose(out);
    return 1; // Success
}
CLASSIC CP UTILITY
The foundational engine behind the Unix `cp` command. Replicates any text or binary file byte-for-byte.
TWO FILE HANDLES
Demonstrates coordinating two active streams simultaneously (input source and output destination).
atom 09 · line file io

LINE FILE I/O — FGETS & FPUTS

unit5_atom_009.c
char line[256];
FILE *fp = fopen("config.ini", "r");

while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), fp) != NULL) {
    printf("Line: %s", line); /* fgets preserves '\n' */
}
fclose(fp);
SAFE LINE READING
`fgets(buf, size, fp)` reads up to a newline or `size - 1` bytes, preventing buffer overflow automatically.
NULL ON EOF
Returns pointer to `line` on success, or `NULL` when hitting EOF or read error. Clean loop condition.
atom 10 · formatted file io

FORMATTED FILE I/O — FPRINTF & FSCANF

unit5_atom_010.c
/* Writing formatted structured text: */
fprintf(fp, "%s %d %.2f\n", "Alice", 101, 3.85);

/* Reading formatted structured text: */
char name[50]; int id; double gpa;
while (fscanf(fp, "%49s %d %lf", name, &id, &gpa) == 3) {
    printf("Student: %s, ID: %d, GPA: %.2f\n", name, id, gpa);
}
FPRINTF SYNTAX
Identical to `printf`, with `FILE *fp` added as the very first argument. Outputs human-readable ASCII text.
FSCANF RETURN VALUE
`fscanf()` returns the COUNT of successfully matched items. Verify `== 3` to detect corrupted lines!
atom 11 · feof antipattern

THE FEOF BUG — DUPLICATE LAST LINE

unit5_atom_011.c
/* FATAL ANTIPATTERN: while (!feof(fp)) */
// feof() reports true ONLY AFTER a read operation has ALREADY FAILED!
// Testing feof() at the top causes the loop to run ONE EXTRA TIME,
// processing garbage or duplicating the final line!

/* THE FIX: Test the return value of the read function! */
while (fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), fp) != NULL) { /* Safe! */ }
THE DUPLICATE LINE BUG
One of the top 5 most common C student bugs. Never use `while(!feof(fp))` to control an I/O loop!
TEST THE I/O FUNCTION
Always control loops by testing `fgetc() != EOF`, `fgets() != NULL`, or `fscanf() == expected_count`.
atom 12 · flushing buffers

BUFFER FLUSHING — FFLUSH MECHANICS

unit5_atom_012.c
/* Force writing cached RAM buffers to physical disk */
fwrite(data, sizeof(data), 1, fp);
fflush(fp); /* Forces OS to commit data to disk immediately! */

// Essential for high-reliability logging before dangerous operations!
RAM TO DISK SYNC
Operating systems buffer file writes to prevent slow disk I/O. `fflush()` forces immediate write-through.
CRASH INTEGRITY
If power is lost immediately after `fflush()`, data is guaranteed to be physically saved on disk.
atom 13 · error checking

I/O STATUS FLAGS — FERROR & CLEARERR

unit5_atom_013.c
if (ferror(fp)) {
    fprintf(stderr, "Unrecoverable hardware read error!\n");
    clearerr(fp); /* Clear error indicator */
}
FERROR INSPECTION
`ferror(fp)` checks if the file stream encountered an I/O hardware error (e.g. disk disconnected).
STREAM CLEARING
`clearerr(fp)` resets both the EOF and error status flags for that stream.

atom 15 · binary files concept

BINARY FILES — RAW MEMORY SERIALIZATION

unit5_atom_015.c
/* Text vs Binary representation of integer 12345678: */
// Text file:   "12345678" -> 8 ASCII bytes ('1', '2', '3', etc.)
// Binary file: 0x00BC614E -> EXACTLY 4 BYTES (Raw memory copy!)

// Binary files are smaller, 100% exact, and 10x faster!
ZERO CONVERSION OVERHEAD
Binary I/O dumps variables from RAM directly to disk without slow string formatting conversions.
EXACT FLOATING POINT
Floating point numbers saved in binary retain 100% of their IEEE-754 precision without decimal roundoff truncation.
atom 16 · binary modes

BINARY OPEN MODES — THE "B" SPECIFIER

unit5_atom_016.c
/* Must include 'b' in mode string: */
FILE *fb1 = fopen("data.bin", "rb");  /* Read binary */
FILE *fb2 = fopen("data.bin", "wb");  /* Write binary (Truncate) */
FILE *fb3 = fopen("data.bin", "ab");  /* Append binary */
FILE *fb4 = fopen("data.bin", "rb+"); /* Read/Write binary */
WHY "b" MATTERS
On Windows, text mode translates `\n` into `\r\n` (CRLF). In binary mode, bytes are written exactly as-is without translation!
PORTABILITY DISCIPLINE
Always specify `"rb"` or `"wb"` when processing binary data, images, audio, or database records.
atom 17 · fwrite syntax

WRITING BINARY DATA — THE FWRITE FUNCTION

unit5_atom_017.c
/* size_t fwrite(const void *ptr, size_t size, size_t count, FILE *fp); */
int data[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

/* Writes 5 integers (20 bytes) to disk in ONE disk write! */
size_t written = fwrite(data, sizeof(int), 5, fp);
if (written < 5) perror("Incomplete disk write!");
THE 4 ARGUMENTS
(1) Pointer to memory buffer, (2) Size of each item in bytes, (3) Number of items, (4) File stream pointer.
RETURN VALUE VERIFICATION
`fwrite` returns the count of items successfully written. If `written < count`, the disk is full or errored.
atom 18 · fread syntax

READING BINARY DATA — THE FREAD FUNCTION

unit5_atom_018.c
/* size_t fread(void *ptr, size_t size, size_t count, FILE *fp); */
int buffer[5];

/* Reads 5 integers directly from disk into RAM buffer */
size_t read_count = fread(buffer, sizeof(int), 5, fp);

printf("Loaded %zu integers successfully\n", read_count);
DIRECT MEMORY LOAD
Loads raw binary bytes straight into the array buffer with zero parsing overhead.
EOF DETECTION
When reaching the end of the file, `fread` returns fewer items than requested (`read_count < count`).
atom 19 · serializing structs

STRUCT SERIALIZATION — WRITING RECORDS TO DISK

unit5_atom_019.c
typedef struct {
    int    id;
    char   name[32];
    double balance;
} Account;

Account acc = {1001, "Alice Smith", 5420.50};
/* Writes the entire struct to disk in a single CPU call! */
fwrite(&acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp);
WHOLE STRUCT PERSISTENCE
Writes all fields (id, name, balance) to disk in their exact binary memory layout.
INSTANT DISK DUMP
No string formatting or delimiter parsing needed. The entire record is written in 1 instruction.
atom 20 · deserializing structs

STRUCT DESERIALIZATION — READING RECORDS FROM DISK

unit5_atom_020.c
Account loaded_acc;

/* Reads the entire struct back into memory! */
if (fread(&loaded_acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp) == 1) {
    printf("Account %d: %s (Balance: $%.2f)\n", 
           loaded_acc.id, loaded_acc.name, loaded_acc.balance);
}
EXACT MEMORY RESTORATION
Populates all struct fields instantly from disk.
RECORD COUNT CHECK
Verifying `== 1` guarantees the full record was retrieved without hitting EOF.
atom 21 · array of structs binary io

BATCH STRUCT I/O — ENTIRE DATABASE PERSISTENCE

unit5_atom_021.c
#define  N 100
Account bank[N];

/* Save entire table of 100 records to disk in ONE call! */
fwrite(bank, sizeof(Account), N, fp);

/* Load entire table of 100 records from disk in ONE call! */

BLAZING FAST DATABASE LOAD
Loads 100,000 records in a fraction of a millisecond directly into RAM.

Utilizes the maximum sequential read/write bandwidth of modern NVMe SSDs.

atom 23 · endianness portability

ENDIANNESS HAZARDS — BINARY PORTABILITY

unit5_atom_023.c
/* Little-Endian (x86, ARM) vs Big-Endian (Network, Mainframe) */
// Integer 0x12345678 in memory:
// Little-Endian (Least significant byte first): [ 78 ] [ 56 ] [ 34 ] [ 12 ]
// Big-Endian    (Most significant byte first):  [ 12 ] [ 34 ] [ 56 ] [ 78 ]

// Binary files written on Little-Endian cannot be naively read on Big-Endian!
BYTE ORDERING
Different CPU architectures store integers in different byte orders. A classic portability hurdle.
NETWORK BYTE ORDER
Standard protocols convert integers using `htonl()` and `ntohl()` to enforce Big-Endian consistency across networks.
atom 24 · padding portability

STRUCT PADDING ON DISK — PORTABILITY TRAP

unit5_atom_024.c
/* DANGER: Compiling with different compilers or flags */
// Compiler A may insert 2 padding bytes; Compiler B may insert 4!
// Direct struct dumping is ideal for same-machine persistence,
// but cross-platform protocols require explicit serialization or packed structs!
COMPILER ALIGNMENT
Different compilers or 32-bit vs 64-bit builds may align struct members differently, changing `sizeof(struct)`.
EXPLICIT PROTOCOLS
Enterprise file formats (PNG, MP4, SQLite) specify exact byte layouts without relying on compiler struct padding.

atom 26 · binary io pitfalls

BINARY I/O PITFALLS — POINTER SERIALIZATION

unit5_atom_026.c
/* FATAL BUG: Saving a struct containing a POINTER to disk! */
typedef struct {
    int id;
    char *name; // POINTER! Stores a temporary RAM address!
} BadRecord;

// Writing BadRecord writes the RAM ADDRESS, NOT the string text!
// When loaded next month, that address points to invalid memory -> CRASH!
NEVER DUMP POINTERS TO DISK
Memory addresses are meaningless once a program terminates. Never write raw pointers to files!
USE FIXED CHAR ARRAYS
Always use fixed-size character arrays (`char name[32];`) inside structures intended for binary file serialization.

MAXIMUM THROUGHPUT
Binary files provide raw hardware speed and compact disk utilization.
READY FOR RANDOM ACCESS
Now we examine how to jump directly to any record on disk without reading the file from the start!
atom 28 · random access concept

RANDOM ACCESS — O(1) DISK INDEXING

unit5_atom_028.c
/* Sequential Access vs Random Access */
// Sequential: Must read records 1, 2, 3... 999 to reach record 1,000! (Slow!)
// Random Access: Jump DIRECTLY to record 1,000 in ONE disk seek! (Fast!)

// Position in file = Record_Index * sizeof(Record)
INSTANT SEEK
Random access moves the operating system's internal file position indicator directly to any arbitrary byte offset.
FOUNDATION OF DATABASES
Allows updating record #50,000 in a multi-gigabyte file in milliseconds without reading the preceding records.
atom 29 · ftell query

QUERYING POSITION — THE FTELL FUNCTION

unit5_atom_029.c
/* long ftell(FILE *fp); */
long current_byte = ftell(fp);
printf("Current file position: byte %ld\n", current_byte);

/* Returns -1L on error */
BYTE OFFSET QUERY
`ftell()` returns the current byte position indicator relative to the beginning of the file (0-indexed).
SEEK POSITION CONFIRMATION
Used to record current position before seeking elsewhere, allowing you to return later.
atom 30 · fseek syntax

MOVING THE CURSOR — THE FSEEK FUNCTION

unit5_atom_030.c
/* int fseek(FILE *fp, long offset, int whence); */
// Whence options:
// SEEK_SET: From the BEGINNING of file (offset >= 0)
// SEEK_CUR: From the CURRENT position (offset can be + or -)
// SEEK_END: From the END of file (offset <= 0)

/* Jump to byte 100 from start: */
fseek(fp, 100L, SEEK_SET);
THE THREE WHENCE FLAGS
`SEEK_SET` measures from byte 0. `SEEK_CUR` measures from active location. `SEEK_END` measures backward from EOF.
LONG LITERAL (L)
Always write offsets with the `L` suffix (e.g. `0L`, `100L`) because offset parameter is a `long` integer.
atom 31 · file size trick

COMPUTING FILE SIZE — THE FSEEK/FTELL IDIOM

unit5_atom_031.c
long get_file_size(const char *filename) {
    FILE *fp = fopen(filename, "rb");
    if (!fp) return -1;
    
    fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END);   /* Jump to end of file */
    long size = ftell(fp);     /* Query byte offset at end */
    fclose(fp);
    return size; /* Total bytes in file! */
}
UNIVERSAL C FILE SIZE IDIOM
The standard portable method to determine the exact size of any file without reading its contents.
O(1) PERFORMANCE
Takes microseconds because the OS file system tracks file length in its filesystem metadata directory.
atom 32 · rewind function

RESETTING TO START — THE REWIND FUNCTION

unit5_atom_032.c
/* Reset stream position indicator to the beginning */
rewind(fp);

/* Exactly equivalent to: */
fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET);
clearerr(fp);
CONVENIENT RESET
`rewind(fp)` moves the file pointer back to byte 0 and clears both EOF and error flags simultaneously.
TWO-PASS UTILITIES
Useful when a program must scan a file once to count records, allocate memory, and rewind to load data.
atom 33 · reading record by index

RECORD INDEXING — O(1) DIRECT RECORD LOAD

unit5_atom_033.c
Account read_record(FILE *fp, int index) {
    Account acc = {0};
    long offset = (long)index * sizeof(Account); /* Calculate byte offset */
    
    fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET); /* Jump straight to record! */
    fread(&acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp);
    return acc;
}
CONSTANT TIME RETRIEVAL
Directly indexes record `N` without touching records `0` through `N-1`. O(1) disk lookup.
MULTIPLY BY SIZEOF
The offset formula is identical to array math: `index * sizeof(Record)`.
atom 34 · in place record updating

IN-PLACE RECORD UPDATES — DIRECT DISK MUTATION

unit5_atom_034.c
void update_balance(FILE *fp, int index, double new_bal) {
    long offset = (long)index * sizeof(Account);
    Account acc;
    
    fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET);
    fread(&acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp); /* Read existing */
    
    acc.balance = new_bal; /* Update field */
    
    fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET); /* Rewind to start of THIS record! */
    fwrite(&acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp); /* Overwrite in-place! */
}
READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON DISK
Reads record, modifies field in RAM, seeks back to the same offset, and overwrites the exact bytes on disk!
MUST SEEK BEFORE WRITE
Reading advances the file cursor past the record! You MUST re-seek to `offset` before executing `fwrite`!
atom 35 · appending records

APPENDING RECORDS — GROWING THE DATABASE

unit5_atom_035.c
void append_record(FILE *fp, const Account *new_acc) {
    fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_END); /* Seek to current end of file */
    fwrite(new_acc, sizeof(Account), 1, fp);
}
EXPANDING TABLE
Appends a new record to the end of the binary file, increasing file size by `sizeof(Record)`.
PERSISTENT AUTONOMY
The new record is immediately addressable by index `old_count`.
atom 36 · sequential database search

SEARCHING DATABASE — SEQUENTIAL RECORD SCAN

unit5_atom_036.c
int find_record_by_id(FILE *fp, int target_id, Account *result) {
    rewind(fp);
    Account temp;
    int index = 0;
    
    while (fread(&temp, sizeof(Account), 1, fp) == 1) {
        if (temp.id == target_id) {
            *result = temp;
            return index; /* Found at record index! */
        }
        index++;
    }
    return -1; /* Not found */
}
LINEAR SCAN ON DISK
Reads records sequentially until a matching ID is encountered.
RETURNS DISK INDEX
Returning `index` enables subsequent O(1) in-place modification via `update_balance()`.
atom 37 · binary search on disk

BINARY SEARCH ON DISK — O(log N) ON SORTED FILE

unit5_atom_037.c
int bin_search_file(FILE *fp, int target_id, int total_records, Account *res) {
    int low = 0, high = total_records - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        fseek(fp, (long)mid * sizeof(Account), SEEK_SET);
        fread(res, sizeof(Account), 1, fp);
        
        if (res->id == target_id)      return mid;
        else if (res->id < target_id)  low = mid + 1;
        else                           high = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
DATABASE INDEXING
Executes binary search directly on disk! Locates any record in a 1,000,000-record file in under 20 disk seeks.
PRECONDITION: SORTED BY KEY
The binary file records must be maintained in ascending order of the search key.
atom 38 · tombstone deletion

RECORD DELETION — TOMBSTONE FLAGS

unit5_atom_038.c
/* Deleting in binary files: Mark with a tombstone flag! */
typedef struct {
    int id; char name[32]; double balance;
    int is_deleted; /* 1 if deleted, 0 if active */
} DbRecord;

void soft_delete(FILE *fp, int index) {
    DbRecord r;
    fseek(fp, (long)index * sizeof(DbRecord), SEEK_SET);
    fread(&r, sizeof(DbRecord), 1, fp);
    r.is_deleted = 1; /* Mark as deleted */
    fseek(fp, (long)index * sizeof(DbRecord), SEEK_SET);
    fwrite(&r, sizeof(DbRecord), 1, fp);
}
LOGICAL DELETION (TOMBSTONE)
Physically removing bytes from the middle of a file requires rewriting the entire file! Marking a flag is O(1) instant.
DELETED RECORD REUSE
Subsequent inserts can scan for `is_deleted == 1` and reuse the vacant disk slot immediately.
atom 39 · compaction utility

FILE COMPACTION — PHYSICAL DELETION

unit5_atom_039.c
void compact_database(const char *db_file) {
    FILE *in = fopen(db_file, "rb");
    FILE *temp = fopen("temp.db", "wb");
    DbRecord r;
    
    while (fread(&r, sizeof(DbRecord), 1, in) == 1) {
        if (!r.is_deleted) {
            fwrite(&r, sizeof(DbRecord), 1, temp); /* Copy only active */
        }
    }
    fclose(in); fclose(temp);
    remove(db_file);                 /* Delete old */
    rename("temp.db", db_file);       /* Promote temp to active */
}
PURGING TOMBSTONES
Periodically copies active records to a new file, reclaiming disk space and defragmenting storage.
ATOMIC DATABASE MIGRATION
Standard maintenance procedure used by SQLite and enterprise databases.
atom 40 · searching foundations

SEARCHING TECHNIQUES — THE LOOKUP PROBLEM

unit5_atom_040.c
/* Searching: Locating a target element in a dataset */

atom 42 · linear search algorithm

LINEAR SEARCH — THE COMPLETE ALGORITHM

unit5_atom_042.c
int linear_search(const int arr[], int n, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) {
            return i; /* Found! Return matching index */
        }
    }
    return -1; /* Exhausted array without match */
}
ALGORITHM WALKTHROUGH
Compares target against element 0, then element 1, element 2... until finding a match or exhausting the array.
ZERO MEMORY OVERHEAD
Space complexity is O(1): uses no extra RAM beyond a single loop counter variable.

atom 45 · sentinel search detail

SENTINEL SEARCH — ELIMINATING BOUND CHECKS

unit5_atom_045.c
int sentinel_search(int arr[], int n, int target) {
    int last = arr[n - 1];
    arr[n - 1] = target; /* Sentinel placed at tail */
    
    int i = 0;
    while (arr[i] != target) i++; /* Single comparison per loop! */
    
    arr[n - 1] = last; /* Restore original tail */
    if (i < n - 1 || last == target) return i;
    return -1;
}
50% FEWER BRANCH TESTS
Standard linear search executes TWO tests per iteration: `i < n` AND `arr[i] == target`. Sentinel eliminates `i < n`!
TEMPORARY MODIFICATION
Briefly overwrites the last element to guarantee termination, then restores original data.

BINARY PRECONDITION — THE SORTING REQUIREMENT

unit5_atom_051.c
/* DANGER: Binary search on unsorted data produces GARBAGE results! */
int broken[] = {50, 10, 80, 20, 40}; // UNSORTED!
// binary_search(broken, 5, 20); // FAILS! Incorrectly reports -1!

/* The array MUST be sorted first! */
STRICT PRECONDITION
Binary search operates on the assumption that elements to the left are smaller, and elements to the right are larger.

atom 52 · binary search algorithm

BINARY SEARCH — DIVIDE AND CONQUER

unit5_atom_052.c
int binary_search(const int arr[], int n, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (arr[mid] == target)      return mid; // Match!
        else if (arr[mid] < target)  low = mid + 1;  // Right
        else                         high = mid - 1; // Left
    }
    return -1; // Not found
}
DIVIDE AND CONQUER
Halves the active search window on every iteration by inspecting the median element.
THREE-WAY BRANCHING
Tests: (1) Equal to mid (found), (2) Less than mid (search left), (3) Greater than mid (search right).
atom 53 · midpoint calculation bug

THE MIDPOINT OVERFLOW — FAMOUS GOOGLE BUG

unit5_atom_053.c
/* THE HISTORIC 20-YEAR OLD BUG (Joshua Bloch, 2006) */
// int mid = (low + high) / 2;
// If low and high are large (e.g. 1.5 billion), (low + high) = 3.0 billion,
// which OVERFLOWS 32-bit signed int to negative! -> Array index crash!

/* THE SAFE FIX: */
int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; /* Never overflows! */
FAMOUS ALGORITHMIC BUG
Existed undetected in Java's standard library and textbooks for over 20 years before being formally discovered.
MATHEMATICALLY IDENTICAL
`low + (high - low) / 2` calculates the exact same midpoint without ever exceeding `high`.

atom 56 · recursive binary search

RECURSIVE BINARY SEARCH — INDUCTIVE FORMULATION

unit5_atom_056.c
int bsearch_rec(const int a[], int low, int high, int x) {
    if (low > high) return -1; /* Base Case: Absent */
    
    int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == x)      return mid;
    else if (a[mid] > x)  return bsearch_rec(a, low, mid - 1, x);
    else                  return bsearch_rec(a, mid + 1, high, x);
}
DIVIDE & CONQUER ELEGANCE
The recursive formulation directly expresses the two subproblems (left half vs right half).
TAIL RECURSIVE
The recursive calls are tail calls. Compilers optimize them into the identical iterative machine code.
atom 57 · lower bound search

LOWER BOUND VARIATION — FIRST OCCURRENCE

unit5_atom_057.c
/* Find FIRST index where arr[i] >= target (C++ std::lower_bound in C) */
int lower_bound(const int arr[], int n, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = n, ans = n;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (arr[mid] >= target) { ans = mid; high = mid - 1; }
        else                    { low = mid + 1; }
    }
    return ans;
}
HANDLING DUPLICATES
Standard binary search returns any arbitrary matching duplicate. Lower bound returns the FIRST occurrence.
SEARCH RANGE AUDITING
Essential for range queries: finding all elements where `10 <= x <= 50`.

int upper_bound(const int arr[], int n, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = n, ans = n;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (arr[mid] > target) { ans = mid; high = mid - 1; }
        else                   { low = mid + 1; }
    }
    return ans;
}
COUNTING DUPLICATES
Count of target items in sorted array = `upper_bound() - lower_bound()` in O(log N) time!
ALGORITHMIC MASTERY
Solves frequency queries without scanning elements sequentially.

BINARY SEARCH TRAPS — INFINITE LOOP HAZARDS

unit5_atom_060.c
/* PITFALL 1: Omitting +1 and -1 */

// while (low < high) // BUG: Misses single-element arrays! Must be <=
THE LOW <= HIGH RULE
Using `while (low < high)` fails to check the final remaining element when `low == high`.
STRICT EXCLUSION
Always use `mid + 1` and `mid - 1`. Never set `low = mid` without `+1`.
atom 61 · binary search complexity derivation

LOG2(N) DERIVATION — MATHEMATICAL PROOF

unit5_atom_061.c
/* Mathematical Proof of O(log2 N): */
// At each step, search space N is divided by 2:
// N -> N/2 -> N/4 -> ... -> N / (2^k) = 1
// N = 2^k
// Taking log2 of both sides:
// k = log2(N)
// Exactly k iterations to reduce any dataset to 1 item!
RIGOROUS PROOF
Proves why halving search space yields logarithmic scaling.
SPACE COMPLEXITY
Iterative binary search uses O(1) space. Recursive uses O(log N) stack frames.

// STABLE Sort:   Alice (85) remains BEFORE Bob (85)!

atom 65 · bubble sort philosophy

BUBBLE SORT — ADJACENT PAIR COMPARISON

unit5_atom_065.c
/* Bubble Sort Philosophy: */
// Compare neighbors (arr[j] and arr[j+1]).
// If left > right, swap them!
// Repeat until no more swaps are needed.

// Heavy elements "sink" to the bottom;
// light elements "bubble" to the top.
NEIGHBORHOOD COMPARISONS
Unlike selection sort (which looks across the entire array), bubble sort compares strictly adjacent pairs.
CONCEPTUAL SIMPLICITY
The most intuitive sorting algorithm in computer science.
atom 66 · bubble sort code

BUBBLE SORT CODE — NESTED FOR-LOOPS

unit5_atom_066.c
void bubble_sort(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {         // Outer pass counter
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) { // Inner comparison sweep
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                /* Swap adjacent pair */
                int temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }
}
OUTER LOOP (i)
Runs `n - 1` times. Each completed outer pass locks one more element into its final sorted position.
INNER LOOP (j)
Sweeps from index 0 up to `n - 1 - i`, comparing adjacent pairs and bubbling the maximum.
atom 67 · inner loop boundary optimization

LOOP BOUND OPTIMIZATION — THE n - 1 - i LIMIT

unit5_atom_067.c
/* Why 'n - 1 - i' instead of 'n - 1'? */
// After pass i = 0: Largest element is locked at index n-1.
// After pass i = 1: 2nd largest is locked at index n-2.
// After pass i:   The last 'i' elements are ALREADY SORTED!

// Subtracting 'i' prevents thousands of redundant comparisons!
TRIANGULAR COMPARISONS
Instead of `(n-1) * (n-1)` comparisons, it performs `(n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n*(n-1)/2` comparisons.
50% CPU SAVINGS
Cuts comparison instructions exactly in half without changing algorithmic logic.

atom 69 · optimized early exit

OPTIMIZED BUBBLE SORT — THE SWAPPED FLAG

unit5_atom_069.c
void bubble_sort_adaptive(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int swapped = 0; /* Reset flag on each pass */
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                int t = arr[j]; arr[j] = arr[j+1]; arr[j+1] = t;
                swapped = 1; /* A swap occurred! */
            }
        }
        if (swapped == 0) break; /* Already sorted! Stop immediately! */
    }
}
ADAPTIVE LINEAR TIME
If the array is already sorted `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`, pass 1 performs 0 swaps, triggers `break`, and halts!
BEST CASE O(N)
Transforms Bubble Sort from rigid O(N^2) into an adaptive sort with O(N) best-case performance.

// Worst Case:   O(N^2)  (Reverse sorted: N*(N-1)/2 comparisons & swaps)

// Stability:    STABLE  (Never swaps equal elements)

Doubling input size N quadruples execution time: 1,000 items -> 1 million operations; 10,000 items -> 100 million.

atom 71 · bubble sort stability proof

STABILITY ANALYSIS — WHY BUBBLE SORT IS STABLE

unit5_atom_071.c
/* Why Bubble Sort is 100% Stable: */
// Condition: if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) swap();
// If arr[j] == arr[j + 1], the condition evaluates to FALSE!
// Equal elements are NEVER swapped!

// Duplicate items emerge in the exact relative order they arrived.
PRESERVING TIES
Because strict greater-than `>` is used, adjacent duplicates never leapfrog each other.
ACCIDENTAL INSTABILITY
Writing `if (arr[j] >= arr[j+1])` would swap duplicates, destroying stability! Always use `>`.
atom 72 · bubble sort on strings

SORTING STRINGS — ALPHABETICAL ORDER

unit5_atom_072.c
void sort_strings(char *arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (strcmp(arr[j], arr[j + 1]) > 0) {
                /* Swap pointers to strings (Fast!) */
                char *temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }
}
POINTER SWAPPING
Notice it swaps 8-byte `char*` pointers, NOT the actual character text! Extremely fast and memory efficient.
STRCMP INTEGRATION
`strcmp > 0` indicates lexicographical inversion (e.g. "Zebra" > "Apple"), triggering the swap.

COCKTAIL SHAKER SORT — BIDIRECTIONAL BUBBLE

unit5_atom_073.c
/* Traverses forward (bubbling max) AND backward (bubbling min) */
// Solves the "Turtles" problem: small values near the end of the array
// that take N passes to move to the front in standard bubble sort!

Alternates left-to-right pass with right-to-left pass.
THE TURTLE PROBLEM
Large items near start move to back instantly ("rabbits"), but small items near end move left 1 slot per pass ("turtles"). Shaker fixes this.

SELECTION SORT CONCEPT — FINDING THE SMALLEST

unit5_atom_076.c
/* Selection Sort Philosophy: */
// Divide array into Sorted Prefix and Unsorted Suffix.
// Find the MINIMUM element in the unsorted suffix.
// Swap it with the first element of the unsorted suffix!

// Repeats N-1 times. Exactly ONE swap per pass!
MINIMUM SELECTION
Scans the remaining unsorted numbers, identifies the smallest value, and puts it in its correct slot.
MINIMAL MEMORY WRITES
Performs at most N - 1 swaps in total! Ideal when writing to storage is expensive.
atom 77 · selection sort algorithm

SELECTION SORT CODE — THE CANONICAL ALGORITHM

unit5_atom_077.c
void selection_sort(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int min_idx = i; /* Assume first unsorted is minimum */
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (arr[j] < arr[min_idx]) {
                min_idx = j; /* Found smaller element! */
            }
        }
        /* Swap minimum into position i (at most 1 swap per pass!) */
        if (min_idx != i) {
            int temp = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[min_idx]; arr[min_idx] = temp;
        }
    }
}
OUTER LOOP (i)
Marks the boundary between sorted prefix `[0, i-1]` and unsorted suffix `[i, n-1]`.
INNER SEARCH (j)
Finds the index of the minimum element in the unsorted suffix.

SELECTION COMPLEXITY — ALWAYS O(N^2)

unit5_atom_079.c
/* Complexity Profile: */
// Best Case:    O(N^2) comparisons (Must scan unsorted suffix!)
// Worst Case:   O(N^2) comparisons
// Average Case: O(N^2) comparisons
// Swaps:        O(N)   (At most N-1 swaps in ALL cases!)
// Space:        O(1)   (In-place)
// Stability:    UNSTABLE!
RIGID COMPARISONS
Even if the array is already sorted, Selection Sort STILL performs `N*(N-1)/2` comparisons searching for smaller items!
MINIMAL MEMORY MOVES
Where Selection Sort shines: exactly N - 1 writes to memory.
atom 80 · selection instability proof

SELECTION INSTABILITY — WHY SELECTION IS UNSTABLE

unit5_atom_080.c
/* Proof of Instability in Selection Sort: */
// Input: { 4a, 4b, 2 } (Two identical 4s: 4a and 4b)
// Pass 1: Min is 2. Swap 4a with 2!
// Array becomes: { 2, 4b, 4a }
// Notice 4b now comes BEFORE 4a! Order of duplicates was inverted!
LONG-DISTANCE SWAPS
Because it swaps across large distances, it can jump over equal elements and destroy original relative ordering.
UNSTABLE CLASSIFICATION
Selection Sort is classified as an inherently UNSTABLE sorting algorithm.

SELECTION vs BUBBLE — COMPARISONS vs WRITES

unit5_atom_081.c
/* Direct Architectural Comparison: */
// Metric            Bubble Sort            Selection Sort
// Best Case Time:   O(N) (Adaptive)        O(N^2) (Rigid)
// Worst Case Time:  O(N^2)                 O(N^2)
// Swaps (Writes):   O(N^2) (Excessive!)    O(N)   (Optimal: <= N-1)
// Stability:        STABLE                 UNSTABLE
WHEN TO CHOOSE SELECTION
Choose Selection Sort when memory write operations are slow or degrade hardware (EEPROM, Flash, SSD).
WHEN TO CHOOSE BUBBLE
Choose Bubble Sort when data is likely already sorted and stability is required.
atom 82 · selection sort structs

SELECTION ON STRUCTS — SORTING BY SALARY

unit5_atom_082.c
void sort_by_salary(Employee arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int min_idx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (arr[j].salary < arr[min_idx].salary) min_idx = j;
        }
        if (min_idx != i) {
            Employee t = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[min_idx]; arr[min_idx] = t;
        }
    }
}
RECORD COMPARISON
Compares the `salary` field, but swaps the complete `Employee` record.
MINIMAL STRUCT COPIES
Because structs can be hundreds of bytes wide, minimizing struct copies to N - 1 is a massive performance win.
atom 83 · descending selection sort

DESCENDING SORT — MAXIMUM EXTRACTION

unit5_atom_083.c
/* Sort in DESCENDING order: Find the MAXIMUM instead of minimum! */
void selection_sort_desc(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int max_idx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[max_idx]) max_idx = j; /* Find max! */
        }
        int t = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[max_idx]; arr[max_idx] = t;
    }
}
LEADERBOARD ORDER
Simply flip the comparison `<` to `>` to extract maximums, sorting scores from highest to lowest.
IDENTICAL COMPLEXITY
O(N^2) comparisons and O(N) swaps.

SELECTION PITFALLS — INNER LOOP BOUND

unit5_atom_084.c
/* PITFALL: Starting inner loop from 0 instead of i + 1 */
// for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) // BUG: Finds elements already sorted!

/* FIX: Inner loop MUST search the UNSORTED suffix: i + 1 to n */
for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
START AT i + 1
The sorted prefix `[0, i-1]` must never be revisited.
INDEX vs VALUE CONFUSION
Store `min_idx`, not `min_val`! You need the index to execute the swap at the end of the pass.

atom 86 · insertion sort intro

INSERTION SORT CONCEPT — INCREMENTAL SHIFTING

unit5_atom_086.c
/* Insertion Sort Philosophy: */
// Like sorting playing cards in your hand!
// Take the next unsorted card ('key').
// Shift all cards in your hand that are larger than 'key' to the right.
// Insert 'key' into the open slot!
INCREMENTAL BUILDING
Maintains a sorted subarray at the left, expanding it by one item on each pass.
ADAPTIVE SPEED
If the array is already sorted, it does ZERO shifting! Best-case O(N).
atom 87 · insertion sort algorithm

INSERTION SORT CODE — THE CANONICAL ALGORITHM

unit5_atom_087.c
void insertion_sort(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int key = arr[i]; /* Element to be inserted */
        int j = i - 1;
        
        /* Shift elements of arr[0..i-1] that are > key to the right */
        while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key) {
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]; // Shift right
            j--;
        }
        arr[j + 1] = key; /* Place key into vacant slot */
    }
}
OUTER LOOP (i)
Starts at index 1 (a single element `arr[0]` is trivially sorted).
INNER WHILE LOOP (j)
Shifts larger elements to the right to open a slot for `key`. Drops out as soon as `arr[j] <= key`.
atom 88 · insertion sort trace

INSERTION SORT TRACE — STEP-BY-STEP SHIFTING

unit5_atom_088.c
/* Sorting {12, 11, 13, 5, 6} (N=5): */
// i=1 (key=11): 12 > 11 -> Shift 12 right. Place 11. Array: {11, 12, 13, 5, 6}
// i=2 (key=13): 12 < 13 -> No shifts needed! Array: {11, 12, 13, 5, 6}
// i=3 (key=5):  13, 12, 11 all > 5 -> Shift all 3 right. Place 5. Array: {5, 11, 12, 13, 6}
// i=4 (key=6):  13, 12, 11 > 6 -> Shift 3 right. Place 6. Array: {5, 6, 11, 12, 13} [Sorted!]
SHIFTING vs SWAPPING
Crucial insight: Insertion sort SHIFTS elements (`arr[j+1] = arr[j]`), which takes 1 write. Swapping takes 3 writes!
EARLY WHILE TERMINATION
Notice `i=2` (key=13): The while loop terminated immediately in 1 comparison because 12 < 13.
atom 89 · insertion sort complexity

INSERTION COMPLEXITY — TIME & SPACE PROFILE

unit5_atom_089.c
/* Complexity Profile: */
// Best Case:    O(N)    (Already sorted: 1 comparison per element, 0 shifts!)
// Worst Case:   O(N^2)  (Reverse sorted: Maximum shifts)
// Average Case: O(N^2)  (Random array)
// Space:        O(1)    (In-place auxiliary memory)
// Stability:    STABLE  (Maintains duplicate order)
LIGHTNING FAST ON NEARLY SORTED
If an array is already nearly sorted (e.g. adding 5 items to a 10,000-item sorted list), Insertion Sort runs in O(N) time!
INDUSTRY USAGE
Standard libraries (Timsort in Python/Java, Introsort in C++) switch to Insertion Sort for subarrays with N < 16.
atom 90 · insertion stability proof

STABILITY ANALYSIS — WHY INSERTION IS STABLE

unit5_atom_090.c
/* Why Insertion Sort is 100% Stable: */
// Condition: while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > key)
// Notice strictly GREATER-THAN '>':
// If arr[j] == key, the while loop HALTS immediately!
// The key is placed AFTER the identical element, preserving relative arrival order!
PRESERVING DUPLICATE ORDER
Duplicates are never shifted past each other. The newcomer sits comfortably behind its earlier twin.
STABILITY MATTERS
Essential for multi-key spreadsheet and database sorting.
atom 91 · online sorting quality

ONLINE SORTING — SORTING STREAMING DATA

unit5_atom_091.c
/* Online Algorithm: Can sort data AS IT ARRIVES! */
void insert_streaming_item(int arr[], int *count, int new_item) {
    int j = *count - 1;
    while (j >= 0 && arr[j] > new_item) {
        arr[j + 1] = arr[j];
        j--;
    }
    arr[j + 1] = new_item;
    (*count)++;
}
STREAMING PROCESSING
Unlike Selection Sort (which requires the entire dataset upfront), Insertion Sort can integrate new items on-the-fly.
REAL-TIME SYSTEMS
Used in packet buffers, live high-score leaderboards, and sensor data ingest.

EXPENSIVE COMPARISONS

atom 93 · insertion on strings

INSERTION ON STRINGS — ALPHABETICAL SHIFTING

unit5_atom_093.c
void insertion_sort_strings(char *arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        char *key = arr[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && strcmp(arr[j], key) > 0) {
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]; // Shift pointer right
            j--;
        }
        arr[j + 1] = key;
    }
}
HIGH THROUGHPUT STRING SORT
Shifts 8-byte pointers rather than copying large character buffers.
FAST ON DICTIONARIES
Exceptionally fast on alphabetical word lists that are already partially ordered.
atom 94 · insertion sort pitfalls

INSERTION PITFALLS — THE KEY OVERWRITE BUG

unit5_atom_094.c
/* PITFALL: Forgetting to store 'key' in a temporary variable! */
// If you don't save 'key = arr[i]', shifting arr[j+1] = arr[j]
// immediately OVERWRITES the value of arr[i] with arr[i-1]!

/* The temporary 'key' variable is strictly mandatory! */
SAVE KEY FIRST
Always assign `int key = arr[i]` before the while loop begins shifting elements.
J >= 0 ORDER
In while condition, `j >= 0` must come BEFORE `arr[j] > key` to prevent reading `arr[-1]`! Short-circuit evaluation protects you.
